P2C00.d: P2C00 reports that a third fuel pressure regulator, labelled C, cannot hold the pressure the engine module asks for, although its circuit tests fine. Letters beyond A and B are only needed on fuel systems with several pressure control elements, for example engines with two high-pressure pumps or separate control of low and high pressure.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power at high load
Extended cranking
c: Regulator C or the pump it controls worn or sticking
Insufficient feed pressure to the controlled pump
Fuel pressure sensor drifting, so the regulator appears off target

P2C01.d: GM uses P2C01 in its 2023 and 2024 summary tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for an engine control module that drives two fuel quantity control valves on the high-pressure side: P0089 covers the first, P2C01 the second, labelled regulator D. The ECM compares the filtered output of the high-pressure controller with fixed bounds.
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Reduced power or stumbling at full load
Hard or slow starting
c: Second high-pressure pump or its quantity control valve worn or sticking
Low tank level or weak low-pressure supply

P2C02.d: P2C02 is the open-circuit check on the control line of fuel pressure regulator D. In GM's tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 this is the second fuel quantity control valve of the high-pressure system, the twin of the valve watched by P0090.
s: Check engine light on
Power reduction because one pump is no longer controlled
Possible rail pressure fault codes alongside
c: Broken wire or loose terminal in the valve circuit
Corroded or unplugged connector at the high-pressure pump
Open coil in the quantity control valve

P2C03.d: P2C03 is set when the switched low side of the regulator D control circuit has contact with ground. GM documents it in 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for the second fuel quantity control valve, where it mirrors P0091 of the first valve.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced engine power
Rough running at high load
c: Low-side wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the quantity control valve

P2C04.d: P2C04 covers the opposite electrical fault to P2C03: the switched ground end of the regulator D circuit is connected to battery voltage. In GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables the circuit belongs to the second fuel quantity control valve, counterpart of P0092 on the first.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, possibly limp mode
Engine may hesitate under load
c: Low-side wire shorted to a supply voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2C05.d: Engines with switchable cam lobes use small solenoid actuators that push a pin into a groove of a sliding cam sleeve; a feedback signal confirms that the pin has moved. P2C05 is the general circuit fault for feedback A on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Cam lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable, slightly reduced power or economy
With harness damage, many other codes and possibly no start
c: Engine harness chafed, sometimes with blown fuses (GM L3B bulletins)
Loose or corroded connector at the profile actuator
Open circuit inside the actuator or its feedback element

P2C06.d: P2C06 deals with a feedback signal that is electrically intact but makes no sense. On GM's 2.7 L L3B, the ECM follows each shift of the intake profile actuator A on bank 1 through three Hall feedback states: extending once the reading falls below 55, extended below 45 and retracted, back at home, above 68.
s: Check engine light on immediately
Lift switching disabled, engine stays on one cam profile
Possible ticking noise from the cylinder head
c: Actuator pin sticking or slow because of wear or dirty oil
Worn groove or sliding sleeve on the intake camshaft
Hall feedback element in the actuator giving wrong values

P2C07.d: On GM's 2.7 L turbo four L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from 2019) each of the four intake sliding-cam actuators reports its pin travel through a Hall element; GM calls the first one intake Hall sensor 1, which is position sensor A in J2012 terms. P2C07 means this circuit is pulled to ground.
s: Check engine light on from the first drive
Engine stays on one lift profile, no cylinder deactivation, slightly higher consumption
With harness damage, possibly blown fuses and many further codes
c: Engine harness chafed through to ground, e.g. over the camshaft carrier cover
Internal short to ground in the profile actuator or its Hall element
Oil or water in the actuator connector bridging to ground

P2C08.d: P2C08 flags a short to voltage on position sensor A, the Hall feedback of the first intake profile actuator on bank 1. GM's L3B 2.7 L four runs this check the other way round from the ground test: the output stage is switched off, and if the line still shows 0.5 ohm or less towards controller power, 4 of 5 such readings above 11 V store a Type A code with immediate MIL (19OBDG03D, again 25OBDG03B).
s: MIL lit immediately
No valve lift change and no cylinder deactivation
After harness damage also rough running, reduced power or no start
c: Chafed engine harness touching a live circuit (GM bulletins PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply inside the actuator or its feedback element
Faulty output stage in the ECM

P2C09.d: Position sensor B belongs to the second of the four intake actuators that slide the cam sleeves on GM's L3B; GM's tables call it intake Hall sensor 2. The sensors are thus one per actuator, not one per lift step: sensors A to C get J2012 codes, while GM puts the fourth (sensor D) under its own codes P30B0 to P30B3.
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
Usually no noticeable change in driving apart from fuel use
c: Loose, unplugged or corroded connector on actuator 2
Wire broken by harness chafing on the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit inside the actuator or its Hall element

P2C0A.d: Here the wiring of position sensor B is intact, but its report does not match what the second intake actuator on bank 1 was told to do. On the L3B, GM follows every shift through three Hall readings: below 55 while the pin is moving out, below 45 once fully out, and above 68 when it is back home.
s: MIL on at once
Engine kept on a fixed cam profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possible ticking from the camshaft carrier or slightly uneven idle
c: Pin of actuator 2 sticking or slow (wear, sludge, wrong oil)
Worn shift groove or detent on the intake cam sleeve
Hall element in the actuator reporting implausible levels

P2C0B.d: P2C0B reports that the circuit of position sensor B, the Hall feedback of the second intake actuator on bank 1, is shorted to ground. GM's L3B 2.7 L uses it with a resistance test while the output is on: at 0.5 ohm or less from signal to ground, 4 of 5 failed samples with supply over 11 V store a Type A code and the MIL comes on immediately (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B).
s: Check engine light on straight away
Valve lift no longer changes, fuel use may rise
c: Insulation of the sensor B line worn through against engine metal
Shorted actuator 2 or its integrated Hall element
Moisture or oil in the connector

P2C0C.d: A short from the sensor B line to a voltage source triggers P2C0C. The sensor is the Hall feedback built into the second intake profile actuator on bank 1.
s: MIL on in the first trip
Cam profile switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With harness damage, further codes, rough running or no start
c: Chafed harness bringing the line against a powered wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply in actuator 2

P2C0D.d: Position sensor C is the third of the Hall feedback elements on the intake side of bank 1; on GM's L3B it sits in intake actuator 3 and is named intake Hall sensor 3. That engine has four intake and two exhaust profile actuators, so a fourth intake feedback exists beyond the J2012 letters and GM handles it with P30B0 to P30B3.
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
No lift switching, no cylinder deactivation
Further codes, reduced power or no start if the harness is damaged
c: Harness rubbed through over the camshaft carrier, wire broken (GM L3B bulletins)
Connector on actuator 3 loose, damaged or corroded
Open circuit inside actuator 3 or its Hall element

P2C0E.d: P2C0E is the plausibility test for the feedback of the third intake actuator on bank 1. On the L3B, the ECM classifies each shift by the Hall signal of that actuator: extending when it drops below 55, fully extended under 45, retracted when it rises above 68 again.
s: MIL comes on immediately
Lift switching suspended, engine runs on one profile
Occasional ticking or uneven running if a sleeve sits halfway
c: Pin of actuator 3 sticking or responding late
Damaged groove or detent on the cam sleeve served by actuator 3
Old or wrong-grade oil slowing the pin

P2C0F.d: With P2C0F the ECM sees the position sensor C circuit of bank 1, the Hall feedback in the third intake actuator, connected to ground. In GM's L3B tables the test runs while the output is commanded on and looks for a signal-to-ground resistance not above 0.5 ohm; after 4 failures in 5 samples at more than 11 V the code is stored as Type A and the MIL lights at once (19OBDG03D; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B keeps the same l
s: Check engine light comes on during the first drive
Engine no longer switches cam profile or deactivates cylinders
c: Sensor C line pinched or chafed against ground

P2C10.d: P2C10 completes the sensor C group for the bank 1 intake camshaft: the feedback line of the third profile actuator is shorted to voltage. GM's L3B logic switches the output off and checks the line against controller power; 0.5 ohm or less in 4 of 5 samples, with supply above 11 V, sets a Type A code and the MIL straight away (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B).
s: MIL on immediately
No lift change and no cylinder deactivation
With harness damage, possibly stalling or no start
c: Harness wear at the camshaft carrier cover shorting to a live wire (GM bulletins)

P2C11.d: P2C11 watches the electric motor of the DEF (AdBlue) pump from the other side than P214E: its driver output carries less current than a working motor should draw, which points to an open winding, a poor plug contact or a motor spinning freely or not at all. Only GM documents it publicly, in its 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04A/B): the DEF control module flags under 0.75 A while the pump is used as a heater for frozen fl
s: MIL and exhaust fluid system warning in the instrument cluster
No DEF consumption, higher NOx emissions
Speed or restart limitation if the fault persists (inducement)
c: DEF pump motor with open winding or worn brushes/electronics (pump module in the tank)
Loose, corroded or spread terminals at the pump connector
Open or high-resistance control or low-reference wire between control module and pump
Faulty output stage in the DEF control module

P2C12.d: Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft in J2012 terms, and P2C12 reports an open circuit in the feedback of its first profile actuator on bank 1. GM's 2.7 L turbo L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from model year 2019) is the documented user: its tables call this element exhaust Hall sensor 1.
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Exhaust cam profile no longer switched, fuel economy mode unavailable
With harness damage, several other engine codes at the same time
c: Engine harness worn through where it crosses the camshaft carrier cover (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Connector on exhaust actuator 1 not latched or corroded
Open Hall element inside the exhaust actuator

P2C13.d: P2C13 is the rationality test for the first exhaust profile actuator's feedback on bank 1, so the wiring is not in question. GM's L3B tracks every exhaust shift through exhaust Hall sensor 1: the reading must drop below 55 as the pin starts to fire, below 45 when it is fully out and climb above 68 once the pin is home again.
s: Warning lamp on at once
Exhaust lift locked on one profile, cylinder deactivation inactive
Occasional clicking from the top of the engine
c: Pin of exhaust actuator 1 slow or sticking (sludge, overdue oil change, wrong oil grade)
Worn shift groove or weak detent on the exhaust cam sleeve
Hall element in actuator 1 delivering drifting levels

P2C14.d: With P2C14 the ECM reports that the line of exhaust position sensor A on bank 1 is grounded. GM applies the check on the L3B 2.7 L while the driver is commanded on: a signal-to-ground impedance of 0.5 ohm or below, seen in four of five samples with the key in crank or run and more than 11 V, sets Type A with immediate MIL; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B adds a general enable flag but keeps the limit (19OBDG03D).
s: MIL on immediately
No exhaust lift change, slightly higher consumption under light load
c: Signal wire of exhaust sensor A rubbed bare against the head or a bracket
Internal short to ground in exhaust actuator 1
Engine oil wicked into the actuator plug

P2C15.d: P2C15 stands for a short to voltage on the exhaust position sensor A circuit, bank 1, i.e. the Hall feedback of GM's first exhaust actuator on the L3B four.
s: MIL lit straight away
Exhaust cam profile stays fixed
Together with harness damage, blown fuses, no start or reduced power possible
c: Chafed harness letting the sensor line touch a supply wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Short to supply inside exhaust actuator 1
Defective output stage in the ECM

P2C16.d: P2C16 is the open-circuit fault of position sensor B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft. On GM's L3B this is exhaust Hall sensor 2, the second and last exhaust feedback: GM's tables list four exhaust pin drivers (control codes P002A, P2B39, P03F1, P3099) but only two exhaust Hall elements, which matches the two exhaust profile actuators described by GM TechLink.
s: Check engine light in the first trip
Exhaust lift switching and economy modes blocked
c: Plug on exhaust actuator 2 pulled off or not locked after engine work
Wire broken where the harness rubs at the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit in the Hall element of actuator 2

P2C17.d: P2C17 flags implausible feedback from exhaust Hall sensor 2, the position sensor of the second exhaust profile actuator on bank 1 of GM's L3B. The electrical circuit tests pass, yet the shift pattern is wrong: after a command GM expects the reading to pass below 55 (pin extending), below 45 (pin fully out) and back above 68 (pin retracted).
s: Warning lamp on without delay
Engine runs on a fixed exhaust profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possibly a light tapping noise from the valve train
c: Pin of exhaust actuator 2 binding because of deposits or degraded oil
Exhaust cam sleeve not snapping into its detent, worn groove
Low or aerated engine oil slowing the shift

P2C18.d: A ground short in the position sensor B line on the bank 1 exhaust side sets P2C18. On GM's L3B this is the feedback wire of exhaust actuator 2.
s: MIL comes on in the first trip
Exhaust profile no longer changes, small rise in fuel use
c: Harness insulation damaged at the camshaft carrier cover or under the air cleaner housing
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to ground
Water or oil bridging contacts in the plug

P2C19.d: P2C19 closes the sensor B group on the exhaust camshaft of bank 1: the feedback circuit of GM's exhaust Hall sensor 2 is shorted to a voltage source. For the L3B the ECM checks while the output is off; a path of at most 0.5 ohm to controller power, reported four times in five with supply over 11 V, gives a Type A code with the MIL on in the first trip (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B).
s: MIL on in the first drive
Exhaust lift switching disabled
With extensive harness damage, stalling, no crank or blown fuses
c: Harness chafed at generator bracket or coil spring stud, line touching a live wire (GM 21-NA-149)
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to supply

P2C1A.d: P2C1A would report an open circuit in a third position feedback on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam profile switching locked out
c: Disconnected or corroded plug at the third exhaust actuator
Broken feedback wire in the engine harness
Internal open in the position sensor

P2C1B.d: Range/Performance for exhaust position sensor C, bank 1: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the commanded pin movement of a third exhaust profile actuator. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P2C1B.
s: Warning lamp on
Exhaust lift held on one profile, possibly ticking from the head
c: Actuator pin sticking or reacting too slowly
Sludge or wrong oil viscosity in the valve train

P2C1C.d: P2C1C is reserved for a circuit-low fault, typically a short to ground, in the feedback of exhaust position sensor C on bank 1. It is not used in any public manufacturer documentation.
s: MIL on
No change of exhaust cam profile
c: Sensor C wire chafed through to ground

P2C1D.d: P2C1D, the circuit-high code for exhaust position sensor C on bank 1, covers a feedback line pulled towards supply voltage, usually by a short to power. No carmaker publishes a use for it.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching suspended
c: Sensor C line rubbing against a powered wire
Internal short to supply in the actuator
Faulty driver stage in the ECM

P2C1E.d: Direct-injection petrol engines often run a catalyst-heating mode after a cold start, with split injections that need tightly held rail pressure. P2C1E says regulator A, which meters the high-pressure pump, ran out of authority in that phase.
s: MIL after two cold starts with the fault
Rough idle or hesitation in the first minute after a cold start
Often no noticeable symptom once warm
c: Worn high-pressure pump that needs full stroke to reach the target
Insufficient feed pressure from the in-tank pump or a clogged filter
Sticking quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump
Worn pump drive cam or follower reducing effective stroke

P2C1F.d: P2C1F is the underpressure half of GM's cold-start fuel pressure check on direct-injection petrol engines: while the catalyst is being heated, measured rail pressure lags the target by more than a calibrated margin. Table 25OBDG03B uses a 3 MPa gap for desired pressures from 4 MPa up (2 MPa at 3 MPa), the same map as P228C; 10 s of failures within 12.5 s set the code as Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip.
s: MIL after a single faulty cold start
Long cranking, rough running or stalling when cold
Reduced power possible if pressure stays low
c: High-pressure pump with worn plunger or sticking control valve delivering too little
Low feed pressure from in-tank pump, filter or pressure regulator
Leaking or sticking injector bleeding off rail pressure
Rail pressure sensor reading too low

P2C20.d: P2C20 mirrors P2C1F: during catalyst heating after a cold start the rail pressure overshoots its setpoint because the high-pressure pump supplies more fuel than requested or cannot be throttled back. On GM direct-injection petrol engines the measured pressure must exceed the target by 3 MPa or more, on the map it shares with P228D, for 10 s within 12.5 s (25OBDG03B; in 19OBDG03D only 2 MPa from 20 MPa desired); Type
s: MIL after one faulty cold start
Harsh, loud cold idle or ticking injectors
Possible reduced power or rich running smell
c: Quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump stuck in the delivering position
Wiring or connector fault in the control valve drive circuit
Rail pressure sensor drifting so the controller overshoots
Engine control software that needs an update

P2C21.d: Engines with two oil temperature sensors can check them against each other; P2C21 means sensors A and B disagree although each signal is electrically valid. GM runs up to three tests in its 2019 and 2025 tables (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B): after a cold soak (engine off over 540 s or 2,100 s) oil, coolant and intake air must start within 16 °C of each other; the 2025 table also expects the oil to reach 70 °C once enough ai
s: MIL after two trips
Oil life or oil temperature display may be wrong
Usually no change in driveability
c: One oil temperature sensor drifting or stuck within its range
Corroded or loose contacts adding resistance on one sensor
Low oil level leaving one sensor partly uncovered
Block or oil heater use skewing the cold-start comparison

P2C22.d: Full hybrids with exhaust heat recovery pass hot exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and divert it around the exchanger with flap A once enough heat has been gathered. A sensor in the flap actuator reports the flap angle to the engine module.
s: Check engine light
Slower engine warm-up and weaker cabin heating in cold weather
Engine of the hybrid runs longer before it may shut off
c: Water intrusion into the heat exchanger or its actuator (Ford Maverick hybrid)
Failed bypass valve actuator with integrated position sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the actuator under the vehicle
Harness near the exhaust chafed or heat-damaged

P2C23.d: P2C23 means the flap position reported for exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve A is electrically valid but does not make sense – for example it disagrees with the command or with how the coolant behind the exchanger warms up. A Ford patent shows that such plausibility can be judged from temperatures.
s: Check engine light, often after frost
No noticeable change in driving
Heater warms up more slowly
c: Water or corrosion in the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3/4 (Ford)
Worn, sticking or frozen bypass actuator
Flap or linkage in the heat exchanger binding

P2C24.d: P2C24 is stored when the position signal of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A drops below its permitted band. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, an open sensor supply or an actuator whose sensor has failed low.
s: Check engine light
Heat recovery switched off, slower warm-up
c: Position signal wire shorted to ground near the exhaust
Open or missing 5 V supply to the position sensor
Position sensor inside the actuator failed low

P2C25.d: P2C25 is the counterpart of P2C24: the feedback from the position sensor of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A sits above the highest value a working sensor can deliver. This usually points to a signal line touching a voltage source, an interrupted sensor ground or an internal sensor fault that pulls the output toward the reference.
s: Check engine light
Cabin heater slow to warm up in winter
c: Position signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground circuit of the position sensor
Position sensor in the actuator failed high

P2C26.d: Many engines feed their injectors in groups from a switched supply, for example through an injector relay or a high-side driver. A separate sense line lets the engine module read back whether voltage really arrives at group B.
s: Check engine light
Possible misfire or rough running on the cylinders of group B
Hard starting if the group is switched off
c: Open or high-resistance sense wire between injector supply and module
Injector relay or its socket making poor contact
Corroded connector in the injector supply harness
Faulty sense input inside the engine control module

P2C27.d: P2C27 reports that the voltage read back on the supply sense line of injector group B is too low while the module expects the group to be powered. In practice the feed never reaches the injectors – a blown fuse, a relay that does not close, a broken supply wire or a grounded feed – or only the sense wire itself is grounded.
s: Check engine light
Misfire on several cylinders, rough idle
Clearly reduced power or engine will not start
c: Blown fuse in the injector group B supply
Injector relay not closing or burnt contacts
Supply or sense wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted injector pulling the group supply down

P2C28.d: P2C28 is set when the sense line of the injector group B supply shows more voltage than allowed – either above the upper limit while the group is switched on, or voltage present while the module has switched the group off. Common reasons are a welded injector relay, a supply wire chafed against another powered circuit, or a sense wire shorted to battery voltage.
s: Check engine light
Often no noticeable change in running
Battery drain if the relay stays closed after switch-off
c: Sense or supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Excessive system voltage from the charging system
Internal fault of the supply switch in the engine control module

P2C29.d: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation valve of the second charger – the later one in series layouts, the bank 2 unit on parallel twin-turbo engines. It is not the wastegate.
s: Check engine light
Less boost and power
Fluttering compressor noise when lifting off
c: Oil or carbon deposits binding the valve flap or piston
Worn gears or motor in the electric actuator
Bent shaft or damaged housing of the valve

P2C2A.d: P2C2A covers an open or otherwise unreadable position feedback from compressor bypass valve B, the electrically positioned recirculation valve of the second charger. Without a valid feedback the engine module cannot confirm how far the valve has opened, which an Achates Power patent names as the reason such sensors are monitored.
s: Check engine light
Boost limited, less power
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at valve B
Broken signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
Internal open in the position sensor of the actuator

P2C2B.d: With P2C2B the position signal of compressor bypass valve B lies below the lowest value a healthy sensor delivers. Likely reasons are a signal wire grounded against the engine, an open 5 V reference or a sensor that has failed low.
s: Check engine light
Reduced boost pressure
c: Signal wire of the position sensor shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Position sensor in the valve actuator failed low

P2C2C.d: P2C2C flags a position signal from compressor bypass valve B that rises above the plausible top of its range, close to the sensor reference. A signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken ground wire or a defect inside the sensor are the typical findings.
s: Check engine light
Boost limited by the engine module
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Open ground of the position sensor

P2C2D.d: Electrically positioned compressor bypass valves have their end stops relearned regularly so that the sensor reading can be converted into a true opening. P2C2D means that for valve B, belonging to the second charger, a learned stop came out beyond the allowed window.
s: Check engine light after a key-off
Boost control less precise, possible surge noise
c: Carbon or oil deposits preventing the valve from reaching its stop
Worn actuator gear or loose sensor magnet
Valve replaced without relearn or with incorrect part

P2C2E.d: P2C2E concerns the power stage of compressor bypass valve B, not its position signal. Such valves are moved by a small DC motor driven through an H-bridge, and the bridge reports when its own supply sags below a safe level.
s: Check engine light
Valve no longer responds, boost reduced
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes
c: Weak battery or voltage drop on the module feed
Poor ground or corroded relay contacts in the supply
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver

P2C2F.d: P2C2F is stored when the output stage driving compressor bypass valve B signals excessive current or overheating. The motor driver protects itself by limiting current and finally switching off, and reports this to the engine module.
s: Check engine light
Valve stops responding, boost reduced
c: Jammed valve forcing the motor to stall against its stop
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground
Overheated or faulty driver inside the engine module

P2C30.d: On engines whose ignition coils are fed through more than one fuse, the module checks each fuse so that it notices when a whole group of coils loses power. P2C30 points to fuse A.
s: Check engine light
Misfire on several cylinders, hesitation
Reduced power while cylinders are shut off
c: Ignition system control module software (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Fuse A blown by a shorted ignition coil or supply wire

P2C31.d: P2C31 is the second of two fuse checks in the coil primary supply: the fuse B group of coils has lost voltage, or the module believes so. GM's patent on this monitor counts how often the current through the fuse falls below a threshold within a set number of samples before it declares the fuse open, then flags a service warning and stops fuel to the unfired cylinders.
s: Check engine light
Engine misfires or hesitates
Catalyst codes may follow
c: Ignition system control module calibration (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Shorted ignition coil in group B blowing the fuse
Chafed coil feed wire shorting to ground

P2C32.d: A crankcase pressure sensor tells the engine module how the pressure in the crankcase ventilation compares with ambient, mainly so it can detect a disconnected or leaking breather line. P2C32 is the general circuit fault of sensor B: its signal is missing or cannot be decoded at all, without saying high or low.
s: MIL on
Crankcase ventilation leak check not available
Usually no change in driveability
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded sensor connector
Open or chafed wire between sensor and engine module
Engine module input or software fault

P2C33.d: P2C33 means crankcase pressure sensor B delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that the engine module finds implausible, such as an offset from ambient pressure with the engine stopped or values a running engine cannot produce. Two bulletin families name it.
s: MIL on, often together with other PCM codes
Limp-in mode possible on affected Alfa Romeo models
Otherwise usually no driveability change
c: Engine control software needing an update (Alfa Romeo and Maserati V6/V8)
Sensor offset or drift, partly due to moisture or ice in the port
Faulty blow-by (PCV) valve producing abnormal crankcase pressure
Harness or pin resistance shifting the signal

P2C34.d: Circuit Low means the voltage from crankcase pressure sensor B stays under the lowest value the sensor can deliver, typically because the 5 V reference is missing, the signal wire is shorted to ground or the sensor itself has failed. Maserati's bulletin MAS002969/A for MY21 Quattroporte, Ghibli and Levante with the F160 V6 or F154 V8 lists P2C34 next to the sensor-A codes P051B–P051D.
s: MIL on
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
Usually no driveability change
c: 5 V reference open or shorted to ground
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed insulation
Crankcase pressure sensor B internally failed
Bent or corroded pins at sensor or ECM

P2C35.d: P2C35 is set when the signal of crankcase pressure sensor B sits above the highest voltage the sensor can legitimately produce. That usually means an interrupted signal wire pulled up inside the module, a broken sensor ground, or a short from the signal to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage.
s: MIL on
Crankcase ventilation monitor not completed
Usually no driveability change
c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Faulty sensor or outdated engine control software

P2C36.d: P2C36 covers a crankcase pressure sensor B signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than real crankcase pressure can change, while staying mostly inside its electrical range. That pattern points to a contact that opens for moments, a wire chafing on the engine, moisture in the plug or a sensor failing internally.
s: MIL that may come and go
Erratic crankcase pressure value in live data
Usually no driveability change
c: Loose or fretting contacts at the sensor or an intermediate connector
Wire rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly
Moisture or oil in the connector

P2C37.d: Engines with a switchable or electric main coolant pump often keep the coolant still, or nearly so, right after a cold start so the cylinder head and catalyst warm up sooner. P2C37 reports that the pump did not behave as commanded during this cold-start phase, for example running when it should rest or failing to start when flow is requested.
s: MIL on
Slow warm-up and weak cabin heat, or rising temperature when the pump stays off
Overheating warning possible in severe cases
c: Switchable pump stuck engaged or disengaged (clutch, shroud or valve actuator)
Electric coolant pump with failing motor or electronics
Air in the system or low coolant level
Coolant or head temperature sensor reading wrong and misleading the check

P2C38.d: A cylinder head temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor seated in the head metal that tells the module how hot the engine really is, even without coolant. P2C38 is the general circuit fault of a second such sensor, B: the signal is open, shorted or otherwise unusable, without separating low from high (P2C3A/P2C3B do that, P2C39 judges plausibility).
s: MIL and engine over-temperature warning
Fail-safe cooling mode with reduced power possible
Temperature warning even though coolant level and fan are fine
c: PCM software causing false faults (Ford 2025 Explorer/Aviator, TSB 24-2393)
Loose or corroded connector at the head sensor
Heat-damaged or chafed wiring near the cylinder head

P2C39.d: P2C39 flags a second cylinder head temperature sensor, B, whose voltage is electrically valid but whose reading does not fit the engine's state, for instance a value that jumps, lags or disagrees with other temperature inputs. Ford is the documented user, all on EcoBoost engines: TSB 24-2441 and its successor 26-2217 (F-150 2.7 L, 2024–2025) pair it with P1299 or P1285 and an over-temperature warning while fan and co
s: Engine over-temperature warning although the gauge and coolant level look normal
Check engine light, often together with P1299 or P1285
Reduced power while the fail-safe cooling strategy is active
c: PCM calibration misjudging sensor B (Ford EcoBoost bulletins, cured by reprogramming)
Sensor B drifted or responding slowly
Sensor not seated properly in the head or corroded terminals
Genuine local overheating from low coolant or trapped air

P2C3A.d: P2C3A reports that the signal of cylinder head temperature sensor B sits below the lowest voltage the module accepts. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors, a very low voltage would stand for an impossibly hot head, so the usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, water inside the plug or a sensor with an internal short.
s: Overheat warning or very high head temperature in live data on a cold engine
Cooling fans running at full speed without reason
Check engine light, possibly reduced engine power
c: Signal wire of sensor B chafed through to ground
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Internal short in the thermistor of sensor B

P2C3B.d: With P2C3B the voltage from cylinder head temperature sensor B stays above the valid ceiling, which the module would have to read as a head far colder than any real engine. An interrupted signal wire, a lost sensor ground, a terminal that has backed out of the plug or a thermistor cracked by heat cycling are the typical finds.
s: Live data shows head temperature B at the lowest possible value
Check engine light
Fans run more often, idle and warm-up behaviour unusual
c: Open signal wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Sensor return (ground) circuit open or high resistance
Thermistor of sensor B broken internally

P2C3C.d: P2C3C is stored when the head temperature signal of sensor B drops out briefly or jumps in steps that no mass of hot metal could follow, while the samples on their own may still lie within the valid window. Loose terminals, a wire that touches ground only over bumps or with engine movement, corrosion in the plug and a cracked thermistor are the usual culprits.
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Jumping head temperature B in live data
Occasional fan runs or brief warnings without real overheating
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor B connector
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting only at times

P2C3D.d: An engine with two head temperature sensors can check one against the other: after a long soak both should read close to each other and to coolant temperature, and while running their gap should stay inside an expected band. P2C3D means sensors A and B disagree beyond that limit although neither circuit shows a fault.
s: Check engine light without driveability complaints
Clearly different values for head temperature A and B after a cold start
c: One of the two sensors has drifted out of tolerance
Contact resistance in one sensor circuit shifting its reading
Engine control software judging the pair too tightly
Real temperature difference from air pocket or poor flow in one head area

P2C3E.d: P2C3E reports a fault on the control circuit of a fourth fan output: the driver in the engine or fan control module sees an open line, a missing load or an error it cannot sort into low or high. What counts as fan 4 is up to the maker.
s: One fan or fan stage does not run when commanded
Rising temperature at idle or in traffic, weaker A/C at standstill
Check engine light
c: Broken wire or loose connector in the fan 4 control line
Fan 4 relay coil open or relay missing
Blown fuse feeding the relay or fan module
Output driver in the control module defective

P2C3F.d: With P2C3F the module senses the control line of fan output 4 at too low a level, which in practice means a short to ground or, with a driver that switches to ground, a line held there by a fault downstream. Saab's 2011 9-5 workshop data define the matching codes for relays 1 to 3 (P0691, P0693, P0695) as a ground short in the relay control wiring, tested with ignition between 8 and 18 V and the engine above 400 rpm,
s: Fan 4 runs constantly or not at all
Blown fan fuse
Check engine light
c: Fan 4 control wire chafed through to body or engine ground
Shorted relay coil or fan module input
Water in the fan connector near the radiator

P2C40.d: P2C40 states that fan control output 4 is held at too high a level: the line has contact with battery voltage, or the driver cannot pull it down when it should. In Saab's 2011 9-5 the counterpart relay codes P0692, P0694 and P0696 stand for a relay control wire shorted to a voltage source, and the manual adds that a stage stuck on can also occur without any stored code.
s: Fan 4 runs constantly, sometimes after switch-off
Discharged 12 V battery after standing
Check engine light
c: Fan 4 control wire in contact with a battery-voltage circuit
Relay or fan module input failed internally
Moisture bridging pins in the connector

P2C41.d: P2C41 judges the outcome rather than the wiring: fan 3 is commanded on and its circuit checks out (otherwise P0482, P0695 or P0696 would appear), yet the controller sees little or no response, usually through speed feedback from a fan module or a missing current draw. No manufacturer publicly documents this code.
s: Engine temperature climbs in traffic or under heavy load
Weak air conditioning at standstill
Warning lamp or fan failure message
c: Fan blades blocked by dirt, stones or leaves
Worn or seized fan motor, corrosion from moisture
Fan control module does not drive the motor
Weak power or ground supply to the fan

P2C42.d: P2C42 reports that the fourth fan output does not deliver what is asked of it: the fan stays still or reaches far too little speed while its control line shows no electrical fault (those would be P2C3E to P2C40). No manufacturer publicly documents P2C42.
s: Temperature warning or reduced power under high load
Fan 4 does not turn when activated with a scan tool
Grinding noise before the fan stops
c: Fan jammed by debris or a damaged shroud
Integrated fan electronics or fan module failed

P2C43.d: Some vehicles split their 12 V system with a switch so that a heavy starter load, typically an automatic restart, cannot pull the supply of control units and displays down. A Ford patent on start-stop cars puts that dip at roughly 5 to 7 V without such separation.
s: Warning lamp or powertrain fault indicator on
Automatic stop-start no longer stops the engine
Radio or displays may reboot during engine starts
c: Open control wire or loose connector at the isolator
Isolator relay coil or electronic switch failed
Poor ground connection of the isolator circuit
Output driver in the control module defective

P2C44.d: P2C44 means the isolation or voltage stabilization stage is wired and commanded, yet its behaviour does not match what the module expects. Ford is the one maker with published cases: 2021–2022 F-150 trucks with the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid and 10R80 MHT gearbox carry a second 12 V battery that an auxiliary battery isolator separates from the main battery.
s: Wrench (powertrain malfunction) indicator on
U061E may be stored alongside
Electrical glitches during engine pull-up
c: Auxiliary battery isolator faulty (Ford replaces it per bulletin 23-2031)
Poor ground in the isolator circuit (Ford GD132, G102, C146, C1989C)
Weak or failing auxiliary 12 V battery

P2C45.d: P2C45 is stored when the line that commands the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch reads lower than its commanded state allows, the classic picture of a short to ground or, with a high-side driver, an open coil pulling the sense voltage down. The switch exists so that the starter can draw its peak current from one battery while sensitive loads stay on a separate, stable supply; Ford's start-stop patent
s: Fault indicator on
Stop-start function unavailable
Possible blown fuse in the control circuit
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Corroded or water-damaged connector near the battery

P2C46.d: P2C46 is the opposite of P2C45: the control line of the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch sits higher than expected, which points to a short to battery voltage, or, on a low-side driven relay, to an open circuit that leaves the sense input floating high. The consequence can be worse than with a low signal, because a switch that cannot be commanded may stay closed during restarts, so the supply dip the
s: Fault indicator on
Stop-start disabled
Screens or radio may reset when the engine restarts
c: Control wire shorted to battery positive
Open circuit with low-side driver (input pulled high)
Control module input or driver fault

P2C47.d: With P2C47 the module saw the command line of the isolation or stabilization stage drop out and come back, rather than stay permanently open or shorted. Loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the isolator or a ground strap that only loses contact when the engine rocks on a restart are typical, and the fault often sets only while driving or on bumpy roads.
s: Fault indicator comes and goes
Stop-start works only sometimes
Readiness monitors may stay incomplete
c: Loose or spread terminal in the isolator connector
Ground strap or ground point with intermittent contact
Cracked solder joint inside the isolator

P2C48.d: P2C48 is a performance check on coolant pump C: the pump is driven, but what it draws or delivers does not match the request. GM uses it in its diesel tables, where pump C is the electric pump of the low-temperature loop: 20OBDG04 estimates the phase current expected at the actual pump speed and flags an error above 4 A for more than 5 s (5 failures in 8 samples), 25OBDG04A above 1 A with the pump over 2,800 rpm (10
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant leak under the vehicle
Higher intake air or fuel temperature, possibly reduced power
c: Low coolant or air in the low-temperature loop, e.g. from a chafed hose (GM 21-NA-265)
Worn, sluggish or partly blocked pump
Fault in the pump's integrated motor electronics
Weak supply from the powertrain relay or poor ground

P2C49.d: P2C49 is the functional check of coolant pump D: the command arrives and the control line is intact, but the pump does not run or does not reach the effect the module expects. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C49.
s: Check engine light
Higher temperature in the circuit served by pump D
Possible power reduction to protect components
c: Air in the loop or low coolant after a leak or repair
High resistance in supply, ground or control wiring
Control module software judging the pump wrongly

P2C4A.d: The clutch actuator position sensor reports how far the release mechanism of an automated or partly automated clutch has travelled, taken at the slave cylinder or inside the actuator rather than at the pedal. Typical designs are Hall sensors reading a magnet on the clutch piston.
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear disabled
Warning lamp or message
Automated clutch may refuse to engage or drive off
c: Damaged or corroded sensor connector near the gearbox
Open supply, signal or ground wire
Position sensor on slave cylinder or actuator failed
Control module fault (Ford internal check P166F)

P2C4B.d: P2C4B flags a clutch actuator position signal that is electrically valid but does not fit the situation, for example a reading that does not move when the actuator is commanded, or end stops that lie outside the learned window. Measuring position on the hydraulic side has its own pitfalls: Schaeffler (LuK) found on its electronic clutch management that brake fluid warming up after a drive shifted the apparent positio
s: Harsh or slipping clutch engagement
Stop-start disabled
Warning message about the gearbox or clutch
c: Air or leakage in the clutch hydraulics
Sensor drift or loose sensor mounting
Clutch end positions not relearned after service
Clutch wear moving the engagement point out of range

P2C4C.d: P2C4C means the signal of the clutch actuator position sensor has fallen below its valid band. Ford documents it in its gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2023 and 2024 under Clutch Actuation Position: the check runs continuously and needs less than one second to register the fault, and in the 2024 version it is reported as base code P2C4A with failure type 11.
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear unavailable
Warning lamp or message
c: 5 V reference supply missing or shorted

P2C4D.d: P2C4D is set when the clutch actuator position signal rises above its upper limit. Ford lists it beside P2C4C in its 2020–2023 and 2024 gasoline OBD summaries: continuous monitoring, under one second to detect, and in 2024 reported as P2C4A with failure type 12.
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear unavailable
Warning lamp or message
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage

P2C4E.d: P2C4E covers a clutch actuator position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the mechanism could physically move. The sensor sits in a hot, vibrating spot on the gearbox or at the actuator, so connectors, fretting contacts and chafed wires are the main suspects; a Delphi patent for such sensors uses two Hall elements and a signal ratio precisely so that changes in the magnet gap matter less, wh
s: Intermittent warning message
Jerky or delayed clutch engagement
Stop-start works only sometimes
c: Fretting or loose contacts in the sensor connector
Wiring chafed against the gearbox housing
Sensor or magnet loose, changing the air gap

P2C4F.d: P2C4F concerns the actuator itself, the electric motor or electro-hydraulic unit that opens and closes an automated clutch, rather than its position sensor. The code means the actuator does not reach or hold the commanded position within the expected time or effort.
s: Difficult or impossible drive-off
Clutch slips or engages harshly
Gearbox warning and limp mode
c: Actuator motor or gear worn or sticking
Air or leak in the clutch hydraulics
Worn clutch requiring travel beyond the learned range
Low supply voltage to the actuator

P2C50.d: P2C50 compares two views of the same clutch: what the pedal sensor A says the driver is doing and what the sensor at the release side says the clutch is actually doing. In a hydraulic system both move together, so a lasting gap points to a fault in one sensor or in the hydraulics between them.
s: Stop-start unavailable
Warning lamp or message
Clutch pedal feel may be soft or inconsistent
c: Air or leak in the clutch hydraulics between pedal and slave cylinder
Release-side position sensor or slave cylinder faulty
Clutch pedal sensor A drifted or misadjusted
Positions not relearned after clutch or sensor work

P2C51.d: Saddle tanks have two chambers and therefore two level senders, A and B; the engine module combines both resistances into one fuel level. GM's bulletin PI0926 for the 2011–2013 Equinox and Terrain shows this layout, with each sender reading about 40 Ω when full.
s: Fuel gauge inaccurate or not reading full after filling
Check engine lamp
Range display jumps
c: Worn resistor track or sticking float on one sender
Jet pump not transferring fuel between the tank halves
Corroded connector adding resistance on one sender
Wrong or misassembled sender after tank work

P2C52.d: Engines with two injectors per cylinder call the second one injector B; with port plus direct injection that is usually one of the two sets, but which one is the maker's choice. For every B injector the engine control learns an offset, a correction for the dead time between the electrical command and the start of real fuel flow.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 1
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 1 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C53.d: P2C53 is the opposite end of the injector B offset learn on cylinder 1: the engine control has lengthened the command as far as it may, and the cylinder still gets less fuel than requested. Ford patents describe the offset as the time the pintle and the driver circuit need before fuel moves, so a sticky or varnished valve or a weak supply raises it.
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 1
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 1, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 1 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C54.d: P2C54 concerns injector B of cylinder 2 and the lower limit of its learned offset. Reaching the floor means the control had to keep cutting the opening time because the injector delivers too much, typically at the short pulses where dead time dominates.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 2 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C55.d: P2C55 reports that injector B of cylinder 2 needs the maximum offset the engine control allows: even with the longest permitted extension of its pulse it underdelivers. Volvo lists it in Technical Journal 36016 for 2022 model-year cars with engine variants L1 and 06.
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 2
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 2, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 2 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C56.d: P2C56 is set once injector B of cylinder 3 has its learned offset stuck at the minimum. How such a value is learned is shown in Ford patents for engines that combine both injection types: with the lift pump switched off, the port injectors fire one cylinder at a time while the others run on direct injection, and how far the low-pressure rail sags after every pulse shows how much fuel that injector really released.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 3
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 3 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C57.d: P2C57 is the upper-limit counterpart for injector B on cylinder 3. A Ford patent on engines with two injector types explains why each injector needs its own learned offset: it is the time needed to overcome the inertia of the pintle and of the driver circuit, and it shifts with battery voltage and temperature.
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 3
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 3, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 3 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C58.d: P2C58 marks the minimum limit of the injector B offset on cylinder 4. Useful for diagnosis is a look at the A injector of the same cylinder: if P02D2 is stored as well, both valves seem to overdeliver, which points to something both learns share, such as the measurement or the cylinder itself, rather than to one injector.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 4
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 4 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C59.d: P2C59 tells that injector B of cylinder 4 has reached the maximum learned offset, so its delivery falls short even with the longest allowed correction. Volvo's Technical Journal 36016 includes it among four codes, one per cylinder from 1 to 4 and all at the Max limit, on 2022 model-year cars; the first step there is software, not parts.
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 4
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 4, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 4 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C5A.d: P2C5A can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders and indicates that cylinder 5's injector B has had its learned offset pulled down to the lower bound. The control has removed as much opening time as it may, yet the cylinder still gets more fuel than intended from this valve.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 5
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 5 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C5B.d: P2C5B is the Max limit for injector B on cylinder 5, found on five-, six- and eight-cylinder engines. With two injection systems, one set may stay idle in parts of the map, and fuel left in a resting nozzle can varnish and slow the valve; the learned offset then climbs until it hits the ceiling.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 5
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 5, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 5 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C5C.d: P2C5C reports that the injector B offset for cylinder 6 has been learned down to its minimum. In practice the most telling check is the learned value itself: a scan tool that shows the offsets of all B injectors makes one outlier obvious.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 6
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 6 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C5D.d: P2C5D says injector B of cylinder 6 needs the largest learned offset allowed. Because the offset depends on how quickly the driver can energise the coil, electrical causes deserve the first look: a corroded or loose connector, chafed wiring or a supply voltage that sags on that injector lengthen the real opening delay.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 6
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 6, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 6 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C5E.d: P2C5E belongs to cylinder 7 and therefore to engines with at least seven cylinders, in practice V8s. It is stored when the learned offset of injector B has been driven to its floor: the valve gives more fuel than the model predicts even at the shortest permitted command.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 7
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 7 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C5F.d: P2C5F, again a V8 code, flags injector B of cylinder 7 whose learned offset is pinned at its maximum. A point often missed is the learn history: when an injector is replaced or software changes, old adaptation values can sit at the limit until they are cleared.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 7
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 7, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 7 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C60.d: P2C60 is the minimum-limit code for injector B on cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8 and the end of this code series. Its A-side twin P02DA is documented by GM for the L5P diesel and by Land Rover for a 5.0 V8, but the B version has no public manufacturer source at all.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 8
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption
c: Injector B of cylinder 8 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)

P2C61.d: P2C61 closes the series: injector B of cylinder 8 has driven its learned offset into the ceiling, so this valve stays short of fuel despite the longest correction allowed. Because a weak supply pump or low rail pressure would starve every injector of the same set, a Max code on a single cylinder narrows the search to that valve, its wiring or the air path of that cylinder.
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 8
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 8, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 8 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)

P2C62.d: P2C62 points to an open trim circuit at the third oxygen probe of bank 1. Wide-band probes such as Bosch's LSU 4.9 carry a trimming resistor in the connector on a pin of its own (RT/IA) that sets each probe's characteristic; the engine module reads it to scale the pump current, so with the lead broken the signal still moves but with the wrong gain.
s: MIL on, usually without noticeable driving change
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitors not completing
c: Trim line broken or terminal pushed back in the probe connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the rear probe
Trimming resistor in the probe connector open (probe replacement)

P2C63.d: P2C63 reports that the oxygen value from the third exhaust sensor of bank 1 has dropped below its physically possible minimum. Despite the trim wording, GM uses it on the 3.0L Duramax diesel for the O2 signal of NOx sensor 3, which sits behind the second catalyst: table 25OBDG04B (2025) fails a reading under -6 percent in 100 of 200 samples on a 25 ms task, with the engine running, supply above 11 V and the sensor re
s: MIL on after two trips
On the GM LM2 often many other codes, rough running or blown fuses when the harness is damaged
Aftertreatment monitors not completing
c: Engine harness chafed or shorted (GM 3.0L LM2 - at the generator or the crankcase pressure regulator clamp)
Third exhaust sensor (on GM diesels NOx sensor 3) reporting an implausibly low O2 value

P2C64.d: P2C64 is the high-side partner of P2C63: the oxygen reading attributed to sensor 3 of bank 1 climbs above what the probe can physically deliver. On GM's 3.0L Duramax diesel the value comes from NOx sensor 3 behind the second catalyst, and table 25OBDG04B sets the code once that O2 reading exceeds 29 percent, clearly more than the roughly 21 percent of fresh air, in 100 of 200 samples under the same enable conditions
s: MIL on after two trips
Further NOx sensor or aftertreatment codes stored
c: Third exhaust sensor (on GM diesels NOx sensor 3) delivering an implausibly high O2 value
Engine harness chafed or shorted (GM 3.0L LM2, PIT5751C)
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector

P2C65.d: P2C65 is the overrun plausibility check for the third oxygen sensor of bank 1: with fuel cut on deceleration the exhaust is close to fresh air, so the reading must land inside a known window. GM's 3.0L Duramax runs this test for sensor 1 under P2297, where table 25OBDG04B compares the measured O2 value with an estimate in overrun and flags a gap above 4 or below -3.25 percent (Type B).
s: MIL on, usually without noticeable driving change
Possibly stored together with other sensor 3 or NOx sensor codes
c: Third exhaust sensor aged or drifting (wrong value in fresh air)
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 distorting the overrun reading
Damaged sensor wiring or chafed engine harness (GM 3.0L LM2)
Leaking injector or model error disturbing the comparison in overrun

P2C66.d: P2C66 reports that pump A of the electronics cooling loop, which carries heat away from inverter, DC/DC converter and often the on-board charger or drive motor, turns slower than requested. Pumps of this kind report their actual speed, and the controller compares it with the target.
s: Hybrid/EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced drive power or slower charging
Electronics temperature rises faster than usual
c: Worn bearings or a sluggish impeller
Debris or sludge in the pump or a restricted loop
Low supply voltage from fuse, relay or ground faults
Air pockets after a coolant service

P2C67.d: With P2C67 the electronics coolant pump A runs faster than commanded. A centrifugal pump speeds up as soon as it loses load, so air in the loop is the leading suspect, followed by a loose impeller or a faulty speed signal.
s: Coolant or drive system warning in the cluster
Churning or gurgling noise from the pump
Reduced power when electronics temperatures climb
c: Air in the electronics loop after service or from a leak
Low coolant level in the low-temperature reservoir
Impeller slipping on the shaft or broken
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2C68.d: P2C68 means the electronics coolant pump A has power and a command, yet its rotor does not turn or stops. Brushless pumps notice this themselves from a failed start attempt or high current with no rotation and report it to the controller.
s: Drive system warning, check engine light
Strongly reduced power or charging interrupted
No pump noise when the pump is activated with a scan tool
c: Seized bearing or impeller in pump A
Foreign matter or sludge blocking the impeller
Coolant frozen due to weak antifreeze
Burnt winding or failed pump electronics

P2C69.d: P2C69 is the general fault for the current in phase X of drive motor A, as the inverter measures it. J2012 places the X, Y and Z series next to the U/V/W codes P0A5D-P0A65 without public explanation; in motor design those letters usually name the second three-phase winding set of a dual-winding machine.
s: Hybrid or electric drive warning and MIL on
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive
Further phase current or inverter codes stored at the same time
c: Phase X current sensor or its supply/signal circuit in the inverter faulty
High-voltage phase lead X loose, burnt or poorly joined at motor or inverter
Internal inverter fault (switching leg or measurement electronics of the X/Y/Z set)
Winding fault in phase X of drive motor A

P2C6A.d: P2C6A means that too little current is seen in phase X of drive motor A while the inverter is driving it, which typically points to an open phase or a dead sensor. No carmaker documents the code publicly.
s: Hybrid or drive system warning and MIL on
Noticeably weaker or jerky electric drive, or drive disabled
c: Phase X lead or terminal open or high-resistance between inverter and motor
Phase X current sensor reading near zero (sensor or its supply failed)
Switching leg for phase X in the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase X inside drive motor A

P2C6B.d: P2C6B flags an overcurrent in phase X of drive motor A. X, Y and Z name the second three-phase winding set of a dual-winding machine, which a Mitsubishi Electric patent shows with its own inverter bridge and a current sensor per phase.
s: Hybrid or drive system warning with MIL on
Sudden loss of electric drive, vehicle may not become ready
Isolation fault codes stored at the same time if the winding touches the housing
c: Turn-to-turn or ground short in the phase X winding of drive motor A
IGBT/MOSFET of the X leg in the inverter shorted or failing to turn off
Phase X current sensor reading too high (gain or offset drift)
Chafed or wet phase X lead touching another phase or the housing

P2C6C.d: P2C6C is the umbrella code for the current in phase Y of drive motor A, the middle phase of the second X/Y/Z winding set. No manufacturer documents it publicly.
s: Hybrid or drive warning, MIL on
Reduced electric torque or jerky drive
Vehicle not ready to drive in severe cases
c: Inverter cannot regulate the phase Y current to its command (control or gate drive fault)
Loose, corroded or overheated phase Y terminal at inverter or motor
Phase Y current reading implausible against the other two phases
Partial winding fault in phase Y of the motor

P2C6D.d: P2C6D is set when phase Y of drive motor A carries too little current while the inverter drives it, the typical signature of an open phase. No manufacturer documents P2C6D publicly.
s: Hybrid or drive warning and MIL
Noticeably weaker electric drive, vibration or humming under load
c: Phase Y lead, busbar or terminal open or high-resistance
Y switching leg of the inverter not conducting (switch or gate driver)
Phase Y current sensor or its supply failed, reading near zero
Open phase Y winding inside the motor

P2C6E.d: P2C6E reports that too much current flows in the Y phase of drive motor A, which sits in the machine's second winding set. No manufacturer documents P2C6E publicly.
s: Hybrid warning and MIL, often with an isolation fault code
Weak acceleration or electric drive switched off
Electric air conditioning compressor disabled
c: Coolant or moisture inside the motor degrading winding insulation
Short between phase Y and another phase or the stator core
Shorted power switch in the Y leg of the inverter
Phase Y current sensor reading too high

P2C6F.d: P2C6F is the general current fault for phase Z, the third phase of the second winding set of drive motor A. No manufacturer documents it publicly.
s: Hybrid or drive system warning with MIL
Reduced electric power, possibly engine-only operation on hybrids
Other X/Y phase codes stored alongside
c: Error in the X or Y current measurement corrupting a calculated Z value
Phase Z terminal or busbar loose, corroded or overheated
Fault in the Z switching leg or its gate driver

P2C70.d: P2C70 means phase Z of drive motor A delivers too little current although the inverter is commanding it. No manufacturer documents P2C70 publicly.
s: MIL and hybrid or drive warning
Loss of torque and vibration from the motor under load
c: Phase Z lead or terminal open or burnt
Phase Z current sensor stuck near zero
Z leg of the inverter not switching
Open phase Z winding in the motor

P2C71.d: P2C71 reports overcurrent in phase Z of drive motor A, the last phase of the second winding set. No manufacturer documents P2C71 publicly.
s: Sudden loss of drive power with hybrid or drive warning
MIL on, vehicle may not restart into ready mode
c: Shorted power semiconductor in the Z leg
Short in the phase Z winding or lead, to another phase or ground
Phase Z current sensor reading too high or noisy
Inverter control software reacting wrongly to transients

P2C72.d: P2C72 says the coolant loop serving the hybrid or EV power electronics (inverter, DC/DC converter, often the charger) does not cool as expected. CARB requires a functional check of inverter cooling performance where feasible, on top of the circuit checks of pump and sensors.
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced power, no EV mode, especially in heat or under load
Inverter over-temperature codes stored as well
c: Low coolant level or leak in the electronics loop
Air trapped in the loop after service
Electronics coolant pump delivering too little flow
Clogged low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan

P2C73.d: Some vehicles split the grille opening into several separately driven flaps; shutter C is a third one next to A (usually upper) and B (lower). P2C73 says flap C stays open although the engine module asks it to close – the counterpart of P05FE, which covers a flap that will not move to its target.
s: Engine warning lamp, sometimes a grille shutter or air flap message
Slightly higher fuel consumption at motorway speed
Slower engine and heater warm-up in cold weather
c: Debris, snow or ice holding the louvres of shutter C open
Actuator motor or gear of shutter C failed in the open position
Linkage or flap frame bent or broken, e.g. after minor front damage
Water ingress and corrosion at the bumper connector of the actuator

P2C74.d: P2C74 judges the drive of grille shutter C: the command to the actuator or the feedback it returns does not fit the expected range, so the flap may move sluggishly, erratically or not at all. Hyundai is the documented user.
s: Engine warning lamp and an active air flap warning message
Flap does not move or moves jerkily
Possibly an unrelated low engine oil message at the same time
c: Water ingress and corroded pins at the bumper connectors of the flap actuator or sensor
Chafed or broken front bumper harness
Actuator of shutter C faulty or responding too slowly
Flap position sensor of the lower air flap faulty

P2C75.d: Smart grille shutter actuators carry their own driver chip and protect it by temperature. P2C75 is that self-protection for shutter C: the module reports its electronics as overheated and stops driving the motor.
s: Engine warning lamp, often intermittent
Shutter C stops moving until the module has cooled down
c: Flap frozen, jammed or bent so the motor works against a stop
Partly shorted motor winding drawing excess current
Internal fault of the actuator electronics

P2C76.d: Shutter D would be the fourth individually driven grille flap. P2C76 reports that this flap remains open when the engine module wants it shut.
s: Engine warning lamp and possibly a grille shutter message
Longer warm-up and weaker heater output in winter
Marginally higher fuel use
c: Leaves, stones or other debris wedged in the louvres of shutter D
Actuator of shutter D failed while the flap was open
Flap frame or linkage damaged by a front impact

P2C77.d: P2C77 flags the drive circuit of a fourth grille shutter D as implausible: the actuator does not respond to its command in the expected way, or the signal it returns lies outside the permitted window. No manufacturer publishes a shutter D, so the code is reserved for designs with four separately powered flaps.
s: Engine warning lamp
Shutter D no longer follows commands
c: Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the actuator of shutter D
Actuator of shutter D faulty, including faulty internal software
Stiff or partly blocked flap slowing the actuator response

P2C78.d: P2C78 is the over-temperature report of the actuator module for a fourth grille shutter D: its driver electronics have exceeded their thermal limit and the output stage has been switched off to protect it. No vehicle with a shutter D is documented, so the logic is borrowed from Ford's smart shutter actuators, which use P05C0/P05C1 for shutters A and B and set them when the controller chip reports more than 140 °C for
s: Intermittent engine warning lamp
Shutter D stops moving for a while
c: Motor stalled against ice or a damaged linkage
Heat soak near the radiator combined with constant repositioning

P2C79.d: P2C79 says the sulfur load held in the NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) has reached the limit the engine computer allows. Sulfur from fuel and oil occupies the storage sites more firmly than NOx, so capacity shrinks until a desulfation is run: rich phases with the trap above roughly 550 °C, as a Volkswagen patent explains.
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from repeated rich regeneration attempts
Occasional rotten-egg smell from the exhaust
Raised NOx emissions, possible failure at an emissions test
c: Desulfation never completes because the trap stays too cool (short trips, idling)
Fuel with high sulfur content (outside EU/US ultra-low-sulfur grades)
Increased oil consumption carrying sulfur-bearing additives into the exhaust
Faulty exhaust temperature or lambda signal that blocks or aborts the rich desulfation phases
Thermally aged trap whose sulfur can no longer be removed

P2C7A.d: P2C7A concerns the second SCR catalyst on bank 1, typically an underfloor brick behind a first SCR stage. GM uses it on its 3.0-litre Duramax diesel: the 2020 table 20OBDG04 compares the efficiency of this catalyst, taken from the NOx sensors ahead of and behind it, with a reference built from the inlet NOx and a calibrated offset.
s: MIL on after one trip
Exhaust fluid or emissions warning in the instrument cluster
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
c: ECM software that flags the second SCR falsely (GM 3.0 l diesel bulletins)
Second SCR catalyst aged, poisoned or with reduced ammonia storage
Drifting NOx sensor in front of or behind the second SCR
Poor DEF quality or under-dosing by the reductant injector
Exhaust leak between the sensors that distorts the NOx readings

P2C7B.d: The turbine inlet valve opens or blocks an exhaust path to a turbine: in a two-stage system it lets gas bypass the small high-pressure stage, in a sequential layout it brings the second turbo in. GM's patent US8276378B2 shows such a bypass valve run in closed loop with its own position control.
s: Reduced power or hesitation in the boost changeover range
Fluctuating boost pressure
Check engine light, possibly limp mode
c: Valve or shaft stiff from soot and corrosion
Loose or bent linkage between actuator and valve
Position feedback that misreports the true valve opening

P2C7C.d: P2C7C reports that the voltage feeding the turbine inlet valve actuator is too low. Electric turbo actuators of this kind combine a DC motor, gearing and a position sensor and rely on a stable feed; BorgWarner's patent on such an actuator adds a spring that returns the valve to a default position when power is lost.
s: Check engine light
Low boost and reduced power
Further turbo actuator codes stored at the same time
c: Blown fuse or faulty supply relay for the actuator
Corroded or loose pins at the actuator connector
Chafed or broken feed or ground wire near the hot turbo area
Defective supply output in the control module

P2C7D.d: P2C7D is set when the output stage driving the turbine inlet valve motor carries more current than permitted. H-bridge chips such as NXP's MC33926 limit motor current and flag overcurrent to the controller, and a Korean patent on electric turbo actuators explains how a DC motor that cannot reach its target draws excess current and is switched off before it burns out.
s: Sudden loss of boost and power
Check engine light, limp mode
Code returns immediately after clearing when the valve is commanded
c: Valve jammed by soot or corrosion, motor stalls
Shorted windings in the actuator motor
Motor leads chafed and shorted to each other or to ground
Defective H-bridge driver in the control module

P2C7E.d: P2C7E indicates that the driver circuit for the turbine inlet valve motor has grown too hot. Driver chips monitor their own junction temperature and switch off beyond a limit, as the data sheet of NXP's MC33926 H-bridge shows.
s: Loss of boost after a longer drive or under high load
Check engine light, possibly limp mode
Fault may disappear after the engine has cooled down
c: Binding valve that keeps the motor under constant load
Partially shorted motor windings raising current and heat
Actuator electronics overheated by missing heat shield or poor cooling

P2C7F.d: P2C7F means the turbine inlet valve's position sensor has delivered an end-stop value outside the window the module accepts during its learning routine. Electric turbo valves are periodically driven against their stops and the reading there is stored as a reference; Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains for wastegates why this reference has to be refreshed, since hot linkages change length.
s: Check engine light
Inconsistent boost during changeover between turbine paths
Reduced power in some engines
