c: Carbon deposits preventing the valve from reaching its end stop
Replaced actuator or turbocharger without a completed learn procedure
Bent or worn linkage shifting the end positions
Position sensor or its magnet shifted on the shaft

P2C80.d: P2C80 says the secondary air pump on bank 1 is turning faster than it should. Newer designs use a brushless motor whose speed is measured: an FCA patent describes a pump with a Hall sensor and target wheel so the controller can infer the air mass delivered from the revolutions and adjust pump speed.
s: Check engine light
Louder or higher-pitched pump noise after a cold start
Secondary air readiness not completed, emissions test may fail
c: Outlet hose detached or split so the pump runs without back-pressure
Damaged impeller or loose coupling between motor and impeller
Faulty speed signal (Hall sensor) or its wiring
Defective control electronics inside the pump

P2C81.d: P2C81 reports that the secondary air pump on bank 1 has become too hot. The pump is only meant to run for a short time after a cold start, until the catalyst lights off, as Hella describes; a pump with integrated electronics can sense its own temperature and protect its motor.
s: Check engine light
Pump stops early or does not run on the next cold start
Hot smell or grinding noise from the pump
c: Pump running too long (many short cold starts, relay stuck on)
Clogged intake filter or blocked outlet path
Worn bearings or debris increasing friction
Moisture or condensate inside the pump

P2C82.d: P2C82 points to a fault in the supply voltage circuit of the bank 1 secondary air pump. Conventional pumps are switched on by a relay; pumps with their own electronics, like the brushless design in an FCA patent, receive a feed and can judge whether the voltage arriving there is plausible.
s: Check engine light
No pump noise for the first minute after a cold start
Secondary air readiness incomplete
c: Blown high-current fuse for the pump
Relay with burnt or sticking contacts
Damaged feed or ground wire to the pump

P2C83.d: California requires every part of an emission-reducing cold-start routine to be checked while it is active and its faults to be stored apart from ordinary ones. Many automatics take part in that strategy: a warm-up gearshift mode lets the engine rev further before each upshift so engine and catalyst heat faster, as a ZF patent describes.
s: Harsh or jerky first upshifts after a cold start
Engine or transmission warning lamp
Shifting returns to normal once the gearbox is warm
c: Clutch apply pressure too high while the fluid is cold
Fill or pressure adaptation for cold fluid outside its target, e.g. after a reset or software fault
Transmission fluid temperature signal implausible, so the wrong cold-start values are used
Pressure control solenoid sticking or overshooting

P2C84.d: P2C84 is the opposite verdict to P2C83: a shift observed during the active cold-start phase took longer than its calibrated limit. Cold transmission fluid is thick, so clutches fill slowly and the engine can rev up between gears; a gearbox module normally compensates with temperature-dependent pressure and fill adaptation.
s: Slow, slipping upshifts with engine flare after a cold start
Engine or transmission warning lamp
Possible emergency program with a fixed gear
c: Transmission fluid level low or wrong fluid specification
Shift valve or solenoid sticking when cold
Worn clutch plates needing more fill volume
Fluid temperature signal faulty, so cold-start shift values are misapplied

P2C85.d: P2C85 means the isolation monitor has found a fault-level loss of insulation on the vehicle side of the battery, in cables or components connected through the contactors. Mercedes-Benz uses the code in the battery management system with the text vehicle-side insulation fault.
s: Red high-voltage or battery warning, do not restart message
Vehicle cannot be restarted after switching off
Electric heater or A/C not working
c: Insulation breakdown in the high-voltage A/C compressor
Moisture in the high-voltage PTC heater or its connector
Chafed or crushed high-voltage cable touching the body
Coolant or water inside inverter, motor or charger

P2C86.d: P2C86 is an early warning that the insulation inside the traction battery, between cells, busbars or module electronics and the pack housing, is dropping but has not yet reached the fault limit. The full internal fault is P0E74.
s: Battery or high-voltage service message, often without immediate limits
Charging may be refused if the value keeps falling
c: Coolant leaking inside the battery pack
Condensation or water ingress through a failed pack seal or vent
Damaged cell sensing or busbar insulation inside the pack
Isolation measurement in the battery controller drifting

P2C87.d: P2C87 is the warning stage for weakening insulation outside the battery, on the vehicle-side high-voltage network. Many systems use two limits; Volkswagen's ID.4, for example, shows a yellow lamp below 510 kOhm and a red one below 90 kOhm.
s: Yellow high-voltage or battery warning
Reduced power or no gear engagement on some models
Intermittent, often after rain or washing
c: Moisture or corrosion in an external HV component (compressor, heater, charger)
Insulation fault inside the on-board charger or DC/DC converter

P2C88.d: P2C88 is the warning counterpart to P0AA6: the isolation resistance of the high-voltage system as a whole has fallen below a first limit without the monitor yet being able to say whether the battery or the vehicle side is to blame. Mercedes-Benz uses P2C8800 in the battery management system of the 295, 296 and 297 model series; its 2025 bulletin lists it with P2C8500 and P2C8700 when moisture builds up in a high-volt
s: High-voltage warning message, sometimes towing not allowed notice
Electric heater stays cold if it is the leaking part
c: Moisture in a high-voltage component that is only switched in at times (heater, compressor)
Gradual insulation aging in cables or connectors
Beginning insulation loss inside the battery pack

P2C89.d: Before the main contactors close, the DC link capacitors are charged through a current-limiting path. P2C89 is stored when the current in that phase exceeds its limit, which points to a short or an unexpected load on the high-voltage bus, a precharge resistor that is bypassed, or a measurement error.
s: MIL and high-voltage system warning at start-up
Electric drive or charging unavailable, engine-only on plug-in hybrids
c: Battery management or DC/DC converter software misjudging the precharge
Short or active load on the high-voltage bus during precharge
Precharge resistor shorted or main contactor closing early
Pack current sensor reading too high

P2C8A.d: Battery interface control modules are the satellite boards in the traction battery that measure cell voltages and temperatures and report them to the battery energy control module. P2C8A says module A is reachable but not working properly.
s: MIL or Service High Voltage message
12 V battery discharging while parked
Many battery communication codes stored at the same time
c: Battery energy control module software or calibration error
Supply dip at the cell monitoring module (12 V battery weak, wake-up issue)
Damaged communication or supply harness inside the battery pack

P2C8B.d: P2C8B is the performance fault for the second battery interface control module, B. In GM's Ultium bulletins it never appears alone: PIP6021 applies only if P2C8B is stored together with P2C8A and the module communication codes U3577 to U35AF, and the 2025-26 versions of PIP6081 extend it through U3584 and add U2BAA-U2BB1.
s: MIL or high-voltage service message
Discharged 12 V battery
c: BECM software anomaly affecting several monitoring modules at once
Weak 12 V battery causing a brownout of the monitoring modules
Connector or harness fault at interface module B

P2C8C.d: P2C8C reports a general fault in the circuit of the fourth temperature sensor of a DC/DC converter, after sensors A, B and C (P0C38, P0C3D, P0E58). Where sensor D sits inside the converter is up to each maker.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Converter output limited, 12 V charging voltage may drop
c: Sensor connector or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor D in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit inside the converter faulty

P2C8D.d: P2C8D is the plausibility test of DC/DC converter temperature sensor D: the voltage is electrically valid, but the temperature it implies does not match what the controller expects. Typical cross-checks compare the sensor with its neighbours after a long rest or look for a value that hardly changes while the converter works hard.
s: MIL on, with newer FCA software after one faulty drive
Reduced eTorque assist or start-stop availability
c: Hybrid control software level (FCA HCP update per 08-037-21)
Sensor D drifting and disagreeing with the other converter sensors
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. low coolant or air in the circuit

P2C8E.d: P2C8E is logged when the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor D drops under the lower limit of its window. Power electronics mostly use NTC thermistors, where a falling voltage means rising temperature; an implausibly low value therefore reads as a converter far hotter than it can be.
s: Hybrid or charging system warning
Converter derated right away, less electrical power available
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Converter genuinely overheating because of a cooling fault

P2C8F.d: P2C8F stands for a sensor D signal stuck above the upper edge of its permitted range. With a thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, the voltage climbs towards the reference as soon as the loop is broken, so an unplugged connector, a cracked wire or a corroded pin is the classic finding; a short to a supply voltage gives the same picture.
s: Hybrid system warning, MIL possible
Electrical power limited as a precaution
c: Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Corroded or pushed-back pin at the converter connector
Signal shorted to a supply voltage

P2C90.d: Under California's phase-in (20 % of 2023, 50 % of 2024, all 2025 models) every PCV hose carrying crankcase vapour must be watched for a break as large as its smallest bore, so makers moved from the general P04DB to per-hose codes. P2C90 covers hose A.
s: Engine warning lamp, often without any other complaint
Oil mist or oily residue near the disconnected hose
Possibly unstable idle or lean mixture codes
c: PCV hose A pulled off, cracked or with a broken fitting
Detection software too sensitive (Ford, Toyota/Lexus and Stellantis updates)
PCV valve or make-up-air check valve not sealing
Crankcase pressure sensor or its signal faulty

P2C91.d: P2C91 is the second hose-specific PCV disconnection code: crankcase vapour line B is detected as open or broken, separately from line A (P2C90). Which physical hose carries the letter is the maker's choice; the code slot exists so that systems with two monitored lines can name the faulty one.
s: Engine warning lamp
Oil residue or hissing at a crankcase ventilation hose
Possibly rough idle
c: Engine control software reporting a disconnection that is not there (Alfa Romeo 2.9 V6)
PCV hose B loose, split or with a broken connector
Crankcase pressure sensor B or its wiring faulty

P2C92.d: The main contactors of a traction battery are relays whose coils are energised by driver stages in the battery controller, and those drivers take their energy from a dedicated supply feed. P2C92 means this feed is missing or interrupted, for example because of a blown fuse, a broken wire or a feed relay that does not pull in.
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Charging does not start
Hybrid or EV system warning
c: Fuse in the contactor supply feed blown
Supply wire or connector at the battery pack interrupted
Relay or switch feeding the contactor drivers not closing
Battery controller input or driver stage defective

P2C93.d: With P2C93 the supply for the contactor drivers is present but does not behave as it should: it sags when a coil is switched on, ripples, or recovers too slowly before the next contactor in the closing sequence. A high-resistance contact or a weak feed therefore shows up here rather than as an open circuit.
s: Several attempts needed before the vehicle is ready
Charging stops unexpectedly
Intermittent hybrid or EV warning
c: Corroded or loose contact in the supply feed causing voltage drop
Weak 12 V battery or ground connection sagging under coil load
Contactor coil drawing excessive current or driver stage faulty

P2C94.d: P2C94 says the supply feeding the contactor drivers lies below its lower limit. Ford is the maker that documents it: special service messages 51513 and 51783 (2023) describe 2021–2023 Escape, Corsair, Aviator, Mustang Mach-E, F-150 and Transit plug-in models whose AC charging at level 1 or 2 stops with the MIL on and P2C94 logged in the SOBDM, the on-board charger module.
s: AC charging stops while plugged in, MIL on
Charging resumes after unplugging and reconnecting
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
c: Supply feed pulled down by a weak 12 V battery or poor ground
Partial short or high resistance in the supply wiring

P2C95.d: P2C95 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2C94: the voltage on the feed for the contactor coil drivers exceeds what the battery controller accepts. An excessive supply is less common than a weak one, but it heats the coils and stresses the driver transistors, and it can mean the measurement is wrong, for instance when the sense line touches a higher potential or the feed regulator inside the controller has failed.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Vehicle may not become ready or may shut down HV
c: Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage
Supply regulator or measurement in the battery controller faulty
12 V system overvoltage from a faulty DC/DC converter or jump start

P2C96.d: Besides commands over the vehicle network, many high-voltage batteries have a separate wired input through which another controller can force the contactors open. The best-known use is the crash signal: in Volkswagen patent US9586481B2 the battery opens its contactor 10–100 ms after a hard-wired crash signal, versus roughly 20–200 ms when the message arrives over CAN, and blocks reclosing until the stored fault has b
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
High-voltage system warning
c: Disable line or its connector at the battery pack interrupted
Sending controller (e.g. crash or airbag module) not driving the line
Connector left unplugged after body or battery repair
Input stage in the battery controller defective

P2C97.d: P2C97 is set when the high-voltage battery's wired disable input sits below its valid range, typically because the line is chafed through to body ground or the sending module pulls it low permanently. Whether low means shut down depends on the design.
s: High-voltage battery stays switched off, no ready mode
High-voltage system warning
c: Disable line chafed and shorted to ground
Sending module holding the line low permanently
Water in the connector creating a leakage path to ground

P2C98.d: P2C98 flags a battery disable line whose level is above the permitted range, usually through a short to 12 V or a sender that drives the line too high. Unlike the low case, the risk here can be hidden: if a high level means all clear, a stuck-high line would no longer pass on a real shutdown request.
s: High-voltage system warning, often without noticeable driving fault
Ready mode may be blocked after the next restart, depending on maker
c: Disable line shorted to 12 V supply
Sending module driving the line above the valid level
Input stage in the battery controller misreading the level

P2C99.d: An electronic throttle relies on learned values: the closed-stop position of its sensors and, in many systems, a correction that widens the commanded opening as carbon narrows the bore. P2C99 says a learned value for throttle A has run into its permitted limit, so the module can no longer compensate.
s: Engine warning lamp, possibly an electronic throttle warning
Idle speed too high, too low or hunting
Reduced power in a throttle emergency mode
c: Heavy carbon deposits in the throttle bore needing more correction than allowed
Throttle body cleaned or replaced without resetting and relearning the adaptation
Worn throttle shaft, plate or end stop shifting the closed position

P2C9A.d: Throttle B exists only on engines with two electronically driven throttle bodies, usually one per cylinder bank on large V engines. P2C9A means a learned value of that second throttle – its closed-stop reference or the airflow correction stored for it – has reached the edge of the allowed range.
s: Engine warning lamp
Uneven or hunting idle
Reduced power if the throttle is restricted
c: Carbon deposits in throttle body B only
Throttle body B replaced or cleaned without relearn
Throttle plate B sticking or its return spring weak
Position sensor of throttle B drifting

P2C9B.d: P2C9B checks wastegate A while the engine runs its catalyst warm-up strategy after a cold start, when the wastegate is commanded open so hot exhaust reaches the catalyst rather than the turbine. GM uses the code on the 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D): it fails if the position error stays above 20 % for over 1 s, the actuator current above 1 A or the duty cycle above 40 %, judged on 25 of 30 samples at 100 ms; Type A,
s: Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Rattle or noise from the wastegate area when cold
Often no noticeable change in performance
c: Wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits, worst when cold
Electric wastegate actuator with worn motor or gears
Poor contact at the actuator connector or wiring

P2C9C.d: P2C9C is the counterpart of P2C9B for wastegate B and only exists on engines with two turbochargers: GM's tables define turbo A as the first in a series layout or the bank 1 unit in a parallel one, so B is the second or the bank 2 charger. GM's 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 (table 19OBDG07, test group KGMXV04.2088) watches the bank 2 turbine bypass valve during the cold-start rapid heat-up mode; if the valve is detected as
s: Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Uneven boost between banks later in the drive
Often no noticeable change during the cold start
c: Bank 2 wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits
Worn or weak wastegate actuator B
Wiring or connector fault at actuator B

P2C9D.d: P2C9D reports that the fuel pressure in the section governed by regulator C stays above its target although that regulator is already reducing delivery as far as it can. A third regulator letter is only needed where an engine has several pressure control elements, for instance two high-pressure pumps or separate rail circuits.
s: MIL on, often after a single trip
Harsh or noisy idle, especially when cold
Reduced engine power
c: Quantity control valve of circuit C sticking in the delivery position
Rail pressure sensor of that circuit reading too high
Wiring or connector fault keeping the valve from being switched

P2C9E.d: P2C9E is the underpressure counterpart of P2C9D: the circuit run by regulator C cannot reach its pressure target even with the regulator already asking for full delivery. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P2C9E, so the detail comes from analogous codes.
s: MIL on
Hesitation or stumbling under load
Extended cranking before the engine starts
Power limitation
c: Worn high-pressure pump of circuit C
Low feed pressure from the tank pump or a clogged fuel filter
Quantity control valve stuck closed or open circuit to it

P2C9F.d: P2C9F concerns regulator D, which GM uses for the second quantity control valve of a twin high-pressure system. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 carry it in an ECM section that also lists the bank 2 rail sensor codes of bulletin 24-NA-106 for the 5.5 L LT6 Corvette.
s: MIL on after one trip
Rough running or reduced power
Further fuel pressure or bank 2 injector codes stored
c: Second quantity control valve (bank 2) not regulating correctly
Water intrusion or fault in the bank 2 fuel harness connector (GM LT6)
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor reading implausibly
Very low tank level causing pressure dropouts

P2CA0.d: P2CA0 is the low-pressure verdict for regulator D. GM bulletin 24-NA-106 names it as a bank 2 low-pressure fault on the 2023–24 Corvette with the 5.5 L LT6 and links it, together with P228C, P01BF, P312B and several injector high-side codes, to an incorrect twelve-pin inline plug with an unsealed cavity that admits water to the bank 2 injector wiring; the fix is inspecting the connector part number and, if wrong, ren
s: MIL on after one trip
Stumbling or misfire-like running
Several bank 2 injector or rail sensor codes at the same time
c: Incorrect 12-way in-line connector admitting water to the bank 2 harness (GM 24-NA-106)
Weak bank 2 high-pressure pump or its quantity valve stuck
Insufficient feed pressure from the tank pump

P2CA1.d: Some electric pumps in a water-cooled charge air cooler loop report back to the engine computer on a dedicated sense or feedback wire, kept apart from the line commanding them. P2CA1 means the level on that return wire stays above its plausible band.
s: MIL on
Reduced power or boost under load, especially in hot weather
Pump fault messages from the pump no longer reach the controller
c: Feedback wire chafed through and touching a battery or ignition feed
Broken feedback wire or backed-out pin, input floats to its high level
Pump electronics no longer pulling the feedback line down
Damaged input stage in the engine control module

P2CA2.d: P2CA2 is set when the return wire from the intercooler pump sits below its valid range for longer than allowed. Insulation worn through against the body, water in the plug, or pump electronics that keep pulling the line down are the usual suspects.
s: MIL on
Engine power limited when charge air temperature rises
Code may appear together with pump speed or performance codes
c: Feedback wire chafed against body or engine ground
Pump electronics holding the line low because of an internal fault
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector

P2CA3.d: With P2CA3 the feedback signal from the intercooler pump is electrically inside its limits but does not fit what the controller expects: a reported speed or status that contradicts the command, a pulse pattern it cannot decode, or a reply that changes although the request stayed constant. Rheinmetall offers auxiliary pumps for exactly these loops that talk to the engine computer by PWM or LIN and carry extensive self
s: MIL on, sometimes only intermittently
Power reduction on long climbs or in hot weather
c: Loose or corroded terminal distorting the feedback signal
Pump circuit board sending erratic or implausible feedback
Interference from ignition or alternator on a poorly routed wire
Pump or engine module software not matching each other

P2CA4.d: P2CA4 means the engine module believes the readings of particulate filter pressure sensors A and B arrive on each other's inputs, typically because connectors, sensors or sensing hoses were interchanged during service. Such a mix-up yields values that look electrically sound but invert the pressure picture across the filter.
s: MIL on, usually right after work on the exhaust or sensors
Regeneration too frequent or not taking place
Implausible filter pressure values in live data
c: Sensing hoses of sensors A and B fitted to the wrong ports
Electrical connectors of the two sensors interchanged after service
Replacement sensor with different pin assignment or range
Crossed wires after a harness repair

P2CA5.d: P2CA5 is the general circuit fault of the fifth temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, the one carrying letter E. Converters measure several hot spots because each part heats differently: a Hyundai patent for a hybrid high-side converter places separate sensors on the inductor and on both IGBT switches, high side and low side, and changes the switching frequency when their readings drift apart.
s: Hybrid or electrical system warning and MIL on
DC/DC converter output limited, 12 V battery discharges
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter connector
Temperature sensor E inside the converter failed
Evaluation circuit of the converter control board faulty

P2CA6.d: P2CA6 is logged when the voltage of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E sits below the lower edge of its window. Converter sensors are usually thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, so a signal that collapses towards zero would mean a converter hotter than physically plausible.
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Converter switched off or strongly limited immediately after start
Low 12 V voltage message on longer drives
c: Signal wire of sensor E chafed through and shorted to ground
Thermistor of sensor E shorted internally
Actual severe overheating of the converter, e.g. coolant loss

P2CA7.d: P2CA7 means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E is stuck above its upper limit. In a thermistor input fed through a pull-up resistor, an interrupted loop lets the voltage rise to the reference, so a pin pushed out of the connector, a broken conductor or a short to a supply line gives this result.
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Implausibly cold converter temperature in live data
Reduced converter output, 12 V battery charge drops
c: Open circuit in the sensor E signal or return line, e.g. pushed-out pin
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage

P2CA8.d: P2CA8 covers sensor E of the DC/DC converter when its voltage is electrically fine but the temperature it reports does not make sense. Typical plausibility tests compare all converter sensors after a long soak, when they should agree, or check whether a reading moves at all while the converter is under heavy load.
s: MIL on, possibly after a single drive
Converter temperature in live data not following load or ambient
c: Sensor E drifting away from the other converter sensors
Sensor E has lost thermal contact with the part it measures
Outdated converter or hybrid control software with too tight limits
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal

P2CA9.d: P2CA9 is the general fault code for the circuit of the sixth DC/DC converter temperature sensor, letter F. Which component this sensor watches is left to the manufacturer.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter output limited, 12 V voltage may sag
c: Damaged harness or poor contact in the sensor F circuit
Temperature sensor F inside the converter failed
Input stage on the converter control board faulty

P2CAA.d: P2CAA reports that the input for DC/DC converter temperature sensor F reads too low. With the usual thermistor circuit this corresponds to an impossibly hot reading, so the controller suspects the signal path before the hardware: a ground short in the harness, moisture in the connector or a thermistor that failed short.
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Very high converter temperature shown even with a cold vehicle
Converter limited or switched off
c: Sensor F signal shorted to ground in the harness
Moisture or contamination in the converter connector
Thermistor of sensor F failed short

P2CAB.d: P2CAB is set when DC/DC converter temperature sensor F delivers a voltage above the top of its valid band. For a thermistor input this is the typical signature of an open circuit, since the pull-up drags the line to reference voltage, or of a short to a higher voltage.
s: MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter temperature shown far below ambient
Reduced 12 V supply from the converter
c: Converter connector not latched or terminals spread
Broken signal or return wire of sensor F
Signal line shorted to a higher voltage

P2CAC.d: P2CAC flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor F as implausible although its signal is electrically valid. With six sensors in one converter the controller has plenty of reference values: after a cold soak all should read close to ambient, and during operation sensor F should rise and fall in step with the load on the part it watches.
s: MIL on, sometimes after a single drive
Sensor F reading out of line with the other converter temperatures
c: Sensor F detached from its heat sink or measuring point
Sensor F drifting against the other converter sensors
Outdated converter or hybrid control software
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. air in the coolant circuit

P2CAD.d: Where a charge air cooling loop has a second electric pump, it carries the letter B. P2CAD reports that the control line to that pump is open, so the driver stage in the engine computer sees no load.
s: MIL on, often after the first trip
Pump B silent; charge air temperature rises under load
Reduced engine power
c: Pump B connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and pump B
Open motor winding or internal board fault in pump B

P2CAE.d: P2CAE concerns the second electric pump of a charge air cooling loop: its control line is held at ground potential where the driver expects a higher level. No manufacturer documents pump B publicly.
s: MIL on
Pump B runs continuously or stays in a fallback mode
Possible power reduction when the charge air gets hot
c: Control wire of pump B rubbed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the pump B connector
Internal short in the electronics of pump B

P2CAF.d: P2CAF says the control line of charge air cooler pump B is tied to supply voltage, so the engine computer cannot pull it down when it switches the pump on. As with the rest of the pump B series, no manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: MIL on after the first faulty trip
Pump B does not start when commanded
Reduced power at high load
c: Control wire of pump B pinched against a 12 V feed
Moisture bridging supply and control pins at the pump

P2CB0.d: P2CB0 flags that charge air cooler pump B is electrically in order but does not work the way its operating data say it should. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
s: MIL on
Charge air temperature higher than normal, power reduced
Unusual whining or rattling from the pump
c: Low coolant level or air pockets in the charge air cooler loop
Worn bearing or damaged impeller in pump B
Kinked hose, clogged cooler or debris restricting flow

P2CB1.d: P2CB1 means pump B in the charge air cooling loop turns faster than it should. An electric pump loses its hydraulic load when the impeller churns air instead of coolant, so overspeed is mostly a symptom of a low level or poor bleeding.
s: MIL on after two trips
Gurgling or a high-pitched pump noise
Low coolant warning or falling expansion tank level
c: Air trapped in the loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Low coolant from a leak in the charge air cooler circuit
Impeller loose or broken on the shaft of pump B

P2CB2.d: With P2CB2 the speed reported by charge air cooler pump B stays below what it should reach. The motor is braked mechanically or gets too little power: a dragging bearing, debris or sludge at the impeller, a weak supply or a high-resistance connector.
s: MIL on after two trips
Charge air runs hot, engine power reduced under load
c: Dragging bearing or sludge slowing the rotor of pump B
Water or corrosion in the pump connector raising resistance
Low supply voltage from a poor ground or weak battery

P2CB3.d: P2CB3 is reported when charge air cooler pump B receives power and a command but its rotor does not turn. The pump's own electronics usually detect this from current flowing without rotation and pass the result to the engine module.
s: MIL on, often with a reduced-power message
No flow in the second branch of the charge air cooling loop
c: Rotor stuck after a long period without use
Debris or deposits jamming the impeller of pump B
Coolant frozen because of insufficient antifreeze
Burnt winding or failed drive electronics in the pump

P2CB4.d: P2CB4 concerns the power feed of charge air cooler pump B rather than its command line: the pump finds its supply missing or outside the window in which it can run. No manufacturer documents P2CB4 publicly.
s: MIL on
Pump B silent, charge air temperature climbs
Other supply-related codes may be stored at the same time
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Corroded or loose ground connection of the pump
Moisture or corrosion at the supply pins of the connector
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the voltage down

P2CB5.d: P2CB5 is raised by the electronics inside charge air cooler pump B when their temperature exceeds the limit; the pump then throttles back or stops to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P2CB5 publicly.
s: MIL on
Pump B slows down or switches off, charge air gets warmer
Reduced power in hot weather or on long climbs
c: Pump running dry or partly in air because of low coolant
Stiff impeller making the motor draw more current
Pump mounted close to hot exhaust or turbo parts
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics

P2CB6.d: P2CB6 rates the boost control loop of charger B as a whole: the pressure produced by the second turbocharger or supercharger strays too far, upward or downward, from what the engine module requests in steady closed-loop operation. It is the B counterpart of P2263 and only applies to engines with two separately controlled chargers.
s: MIL on
Uneven or reduced power under load
Hissing or whistling from the charge air system
c: Leak in the charge air path of charger B
Sticking wastegate or variable vanes of charger B
Restriction in the exhaust upstream or downstream of turbine B
Boost pressure sensor B reading inaccurately

P2CB7.d: P2CB7 states that charger B delivers practically no boost although the operating point calls for it, and that the reason is likely mechanical rather than electrical: the pressure measured after the second compressor hardly rises above ambient. It mirrors P2262 for charger A and is relevant only to engines with two separately monitored boost paths.
s: Clearly flat acceleration
MIL on, power limited
Unusual hissing or no turbo sound
c: Intake or charge air hose of charger B detached or split
Wastegate or bypass of charger B stuck open
Actuator linkage or vacuum supply to charger B failed

P2CB8.d: P2CB8 reports that the second charger, B, produces more boost than the engine module allows, and attributes this to a mechanical cause such as a wastegate or bypass of charger B that no longer opens, a seized actuator rod or sooted variable vanes stuck in the closed position. It is the B twin of P226B.
s: Sudden power cut under full load
MIL on
Surging or jerky boost build-up
c: Wastegate of charger B stuck closed
Variable turbine vanes of charger B sooted and sticking
Seized actuator rod or linkage on charger B
Boost pressure sensor B reading too high

P2CB9.d: P2CB9 means the second electric cooling fan reports a lower speed than its command calls for, while communication and wiring are judged sound. GM uses it in two ways.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant temperature rises at idle or when towing
Weaker air conditioning at standstill
c: Fan blades slowed by debris, leaves, snow or ice
Fan 2 motor or its integrated electronics worn or faulty
Blown fuse, weak supply or poor ground at the fan
Sporadic entry without fault found (GM investigated without a fix)

P2CBA.d: With P2CBA the controller finds fan 2 spinning clearly faster than its own estimate of what the current command should produce. GM documents the check in tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07: the reported speed minus the estimated speed must exceed a margin of 1400 to 4050 rpm, depending on the operating point, for 20 s with more than 9.5 V on board, and the lamp follows on the second trip.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unusually loud or vibrating fan noise
Fan runs at high speed even with a cool engine
c: Fan blade broken or partly missing, less load on the motor
Fan electronics drive the motor harder than commanded
Implausible speed feedback from the fan module
Shroud damaged or detached so the rotor runs free

P2CBB.d: P2CBB concerns vehicles with three electric radiator fans: the third one turns slower than modelled for its command. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes the check for a LIN-controlled fan 3.
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine runs warmer under high load or in heat
Reduced A/C cooling at low speed
c: Fan 3 slowed by debris, ice or a distorted shroud
Fan 3 motor bearings or integrated controller worn
Voltage drop on the fan 3 power feed or ground

P2CBC.d: P2CBC is the counterpart to P2CBB: the third cooling fan turns noticeably faster than the controller expects for the present request. No manufacturer publicly documents this code.
s: Check engine light, depending on the maker
Loud or rough fan noise
c: Fan 3 blade broken or rotor unbalanced
Fan 3 electronics ignore the speed command
Wrong speed value reported by the fan module

P2CBD.d: Some engines heat the crankcase ventilation path so that moisture and oil carried by blow-by gas cannot freeze and block it; engines with two such paths, for example a PCV line and a separate make-up air line feeding the turbo intake, may carry a second heater, B. P2CBD reports that the control circuit of heater B is open, so the element never receives current.
s: MIL on (depending on manufacturer) or code stored only
No noticeable effect in mild weather
In hard frost, iced ventilation path with oil leaks or rough idle
c: Corroded or loose connector at heater B
Faulty output stage in the engine control module

P2CBE.d: P2CBE says the switched control line of PCV heater B carries too high a voltage, usually because it touches battery positive. Since the module normally completes the heater circuit by pulling this line to ground, a short to supply means the output can no longer switch the element on, or the driver shuts down to protect itself, so heater B stays cold.
s: Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B inactive, risk of an iced ventilation path in frost
c: Control wire chafed through and touching battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the heater B connector
Internal short in heating element B
Damaged output stage in the engine control module

P2CBF.d: P2CBF is set when the control line of PCV heater B sits at ground potential at a moment the module expects a voltage on it. On the usual low-side layout, with supply fed directly to the heater and the module providing the ground, a short to ground on that line turns heater B on permanently regardless of command.
s: Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B constantly on, slightly higher electrical load
Usually no driveability complaint
c: Control wire pinched or chafed to engine ground
Output stage in the engine module shorted internally

P2CC0.d: P2CC0 covers PCV heater B when its wiring passes the electrical tests but the heater does not behave as expected: current outside the plausible window, an overheated output stage, or no sign of the commanded warming. It complements the circuit codes P2CBD to P2CBF, which only detect opens and shorts.
s: Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Possible icing of the ventilation line in frost
c: Heating element B with drifted resistance
High-resistance contact in connector or supply
Output stage overheating in the engine control module

P2CC1.d: P2CC1 is the general fault of a second sense line through which the engine controller reads the actual charging voltage. In the charging system, generator means the alternator; a sense input taps the voltage at the rectifier or battery without load current, so wiring losses do not distort it.
s: Battery or charging warning lamp on
Charging voltage regulated to a fixed or unsuitable value
c: Sense wire B, its fuse or connector open or corroded
Second alternator or its regulator faulty
Sense input in the engine control module faulty

P2CC2.d: P2CC2 means the voltage arriving on generator sense circuit B is within electrical limits but does not agree with what the controller expects, such as the battery voltage measured elsewhere, the commanded set point or the reading of sense circuit A. The usual cause is a voltage drop: corroded ring terminals, a loose ground strap or a damaged fusible link make the sensed value lag behind reality.
s: Charging warning lamp on or flickering
Battery not fully charged or charging voltage fluctuating
c: Voltage drop from corroded terminals, loose ground strap or damaged fusible link
Alternator B delivering too little or unstable output
Battery with high internal resistance distorting the comparison

P2CC3.d: P2CC3 is stored when generator sense circuit B reports a voltage below its lower limit, in practice often close to zero. Typical causes are an open sense lead, a blown fuse in it or a short to ground; on Chrysler alternators, according to Remy, an internal 2.4 kΩ resistor shields the sense terminal against such a ground fault.
s: Charging warning lamp on
Charging voltage too high or held at a fixed value
Overcharged battery, bright lights
c: Sense wire B broken or its fuse blown
Sense wire B chafed and shorted to ground
Corroded sense terminal at the alternator or module

P2CC4.d: P2CC4 indicates that generator sense circuit B reads above its upper limit. Either the line is shorted to a higher voltage, or the voltage at the measuring point really is excessive, for example because the regulator keeps the field fully energised; Remy warns that a full-field alternator can quickly push the system above 16 V.
s: Charging warning lamp on
Very high system voltage, bulbs failing early
Battery gassing or smelling
c: Regulator of alternator B stuck in full field, real overvoltage
Sense wire B shorted to a higher-voltage line
Sense input of the engine control module faulty

P2CC5.d: P2CC5 concerns supply B inside the inverter that drives a hybrid's generator (motor-generator), typically a low-voltage rail feeding the gate drivers of the power transistors. Which supply gets the letter B is defined by the manufacturer; a second inverter channel or second generator would also fit.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator out of operation, vehicle may not become ready to drive
c: Supply B for the gate drivers failed inside the inverter
12 V feed, fuse or connector of the inverter interrupted
Poor ground connection of the inverter control electronics

P2CC6.d: P2CC6 means supply B of the generator inverter is present but below its permitted level. A weak gate driver feed is dangerous for the power stage: transistors that are not driven fully on run in a lossy partial state and heat up quickly, so the inverter typically blocks the generator.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator limited or switched off, reduced hybrid performance
c: Internal regulator of supply B delivering too little voltage
Low 12 V input to the inverter, e.g. weak auxiliary battery
Corroded ground or connector of the inverter

P2CC7.d: P2CC7 is set when supply B of the generator inverter exceeds its upper limit. Gate inputs of IGBTs tolerate only a limited voltage, so overvoltage on the driver rail puts the switches at risk and the inverter is normally shut down.
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator blocked, battery no longer charged while driving
c: Regulator of supply B inside the inverter faulty
Short between two internal supply rails
Overvoltage in the 12 V system from a DC/DC converter fault

P2CC8.d: Some engines measure how fast a coolant pump turns with a dedicated speed sensor, for instance on a pump that can be engaged and released or on an electric pump read back by the controller. P2CC8 is the general fault of that sensor's circuit: the signal is absent or cannot be used, without the controller deciding whether it is too low or too high.
s: MIL on
Coolant pump held in a default state, warm-up may change
c: Failed speed sensor delivering no usable signal
Damaged wiring or loose connector at the sensor
Missing reference voltage or ground for the sensor

P2CC9.d: P2CC9 means the coolant pump speed sensor delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense. The controller compares it with what the pump should be doing: a belt-driven pump has to follow engine speed in a fixed ratio once engaged, an electric pump should match its commanded speed.
s: MIL on after repeated detection
Engine may run warmer than usual or take longer to warm up
c: Slipping belt or clutch, so the pump turns slower than expected
Sensor loose, wrong air gap or damaged trigger wheel
Sensor electronics drifting or dropping pulses

P2CCA.d: P2CCA is stored when the signal line of the coolant pump speed sensor remains below its lower limit, so no pulses or levels above the threshold arrive. Most often the signal wire is shorted to ground, the sensor has lost its supply voltage and therefore cannot switch, or its output stage has failed in the off state.
s: MIL on
Pump speed reads zero in live data although the engine runs
c: Sensor supply voltage missing because of an open feed
Sensor output stage failed in the low state

P2CCB.d: P2CCB covers the upper end of the coolant pump speed sensor signal: the input stays above its permitted maximum. On sensors with an open-collector output and a pull-up resistor in the controller, an interrupted signal wire or a sensor that has lost its ground leaves the line resting high, so the open case often lands here rather than under P2CCA.
s: MIL on
Pump speed missing or stuck at an implausible value in live data
c: Open signal wire, input pulled up by the controller
Lost ground connection at the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage feed

P2CCC.d: P2CCC continues the state-of-health series for sectioned traction batteries in the P2 block: after A (P0A7F) and B to F (P0EDD to P0EE1), section G is the seventh. The controller has concluded that this part of the pack has lost too much usable capacity or power.
s: Yellow engine warning lamp on
Displayed electric range too low
Electric driving mode unavailable or ends early
c: Battery module of group 7 lost capacity or power
Single weak cell block dragging the section down
State-of-health estimate of the battery controller wrong

P2CCD.d: P2CCD reports that section H, the eighth subdivision of a traction battery, has aged past the limit its controller accepts. In practice this code only exists on large packs that the battery management splits into at least eight separately judged groups.
s: MIL on
Shorter electric range
Less power in electric mode
c: Battery module of group 8 worn out
Module aged faster due to heat or uneven cooling
Faulty state-of-health judgement by the battery controller

P2CCE.d: P2CCE is reserved for the ninth section, I, of a traction battery whose controller rates the health of each section on its own. The fault is a capacity or power verdict, not an electrical one: section I no longer delivers what a healthy unit should.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Shorter electric range
c: Module or cell group of section I aged beyond its limit
Uneven pack temperature stressing this section
Misjudged state of health in the battery controller

P2CCF.d: P2CCF belongs to the deterioration series that rates each section of a divided traction battery on its own; J is the tenth section after A (P0A7F), B to F (P0EDD–P0EE1) and G to I (P2CCC–P2CCE). It is not an electrical fault: the controller has decided that the modules of section J have given up more usable capacity or power than allowed.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Electric range noticeably shorter
Less power available in electric driving
c: Modules of section J worn beyond the accepted capacity or power limit
Section J repeatedly ran hotter than the rest of the pack
Health estimate of the battery controller wrong after software or sensor issue

P2CD0.d: With P2CD0 the battery controller reports that section K, the eleventh separately judged part of the high-voltage battery, has exceeded its ageing limit. Such a verdict normally rests on comparing what this section stores and delivers with its neighbours over many charge cycles, so it rarely appears suddenly after one event.
s: Warning lamp for engine or hybrid system
Shorter range on a full charge
Weaker acceleration on battery power
c: Cells of section K lost capacity faster than the other sections
Internal resistance of section K increased, limiting power
Uneven coolant flow leaving section K warmer over years

P2CD1.d: P2CD1 marks section L, the twelfth subdivision of the high-voltage pack, as worn: its usable capacity or power capability has fallen below what the controller accepts. The code only makes sense for packs whose management tracks twelve or more groups individually; no carmaker documents it publicly, and the largest published series, Audi's Q5 PHEV, ends with group 8.
s: MIL illuminated
Battery charge falls faster than usual
c: Section L has reached the end of its usable life
One weak cell block pulling the whole section down
Faulty voltage sensing making section L look weaker than it is

P2CD2.d: P2CD2 flags section M, the thirteenth part of a sectioned high-voltage battery, as degraded in capacity or power. Unlike sections J to L, M has no matching over-temperature code in the available code lists, so the thermal history of this section has to be read from general pack temperature data.
s: Hybrid or engine warning lamp on
Reduced electric-only range
Sluggish response in electric mode
c: Section M degraded by age and charge cycles
Long standstill at low charge damaged cells of section M
Cell balancing of section M no longer working

P2CD3.d: P2CD3 closes the lettered deterioration series: N is the fourteenth section of a drive battery whose management assesses each section's condition separately. When it sets, section N can no longer hold or release the energy expected of it, even though wiring and sensors may be intact.
s: MIL or hybrid warning
Electric range clearly reduced
Drive power limited at times
c: Cells in section N aged beyond the acceptance limit
Earlier replaced neighbour modules leave section N as the weak link
Battery controller misjudges section N after a reset or update

P2CD4.d: P2CD4 is a plausibility check between two refrigerant pressure sensors that serve one A/C or heat pump circuit: the module flags it when the pair disagrees beyond what the system allows, even though each sensor is electrically fine. Bentley documents the code as P2CD400 in the thermal management ECU (address 00C5) of 2025 Continental GT and GTC models as well as the Flying Spur; campaign ED35 corrects its handling wi
s: A/C cools weakly or the compressor is limited
Code stored in the thermal management or climate module
c: Thermal management software misjudging the sensor comparison (Bentley 2025 campaign)
One pressure sensor drifting or failing internally while still in range
Contact resistance at one sensor connector shifting its signal

P2CD5.d: Bypass valve C is a third compressor recirculation valve, which only exists on layouts with three charging paths or stages; on lift-off it routes boosted air back to the compressor inlet so the compressor does not surge. It is not the wastegate.
s: Fluttering or surging noise from the intake when lifting off the throttle
Boost builds slowly or stays low when the valve is stuck open
Warning lamp on and engine power limited
c: Valve or piston seized by oil and soot deposits from the crankcase breather
Electric actuator or diaphragm of the valve worn or failed
Missing vacuum or control signal on a pneumatically operated valve
Position feedback reports movement wrongly although the valve works

P2CD6.d: A fourth boost pressure sensor, D, is only needed where charge pressure is read at four points, for example on twin-turbo engines with two stages per bank or on combinations of supercharger, turbocharger and electric compressor. Which tap gets the letter is up to the manufacturer.
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced boost and noticeably less power
Other sensor codes at the same time if a shared 5 V supply is affected
c: Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire at sensor D
5 V reference or sensor ground interrupted
Input stage of the engine control module faulty

P2CD7.d: With P2CD7 the boost sensor D signal is electrically valid but does not fit the other pressure readings or the engine's air model. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the checks used for sensor A show what it would cover.
s: Warning lamp on
Boost limited, weaker acceleration
Scan tool shows sensor D value differing from barometric pressure with the engine off
c: Sensor D drifted or contaminated with oil
Leaking seal or blocked port at the sensor's measuring point
Charge air leak in the section monitored by sensor D
Sensor with the wrong pressure range fitted

P2CD8.d: P2CD8 is stored when the voltage from boost sensor D falls below the lowest value a healthy sensor can output. Since these sensors rise in voltage as pressure rises, a reading near zero almost always points to the electrics: signal shorted to ground, an interrupted 5 V supply, or a broken signal wire that the module pulls low.
s: Warning lamp on
Only base boost available, clear loss of power
Live data shows sensor D at or near minimum pressure even under load
c: Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
5 V reference to the sensor open or shorted
Sensor D internally failed with output stuck low

P2CD9.d: P2CD9 reports a boost sensor D voltage above the highest valid level. A signal pinned near the reference rarely reflects real overboost; more often the signal wire touches 5 V or battery voltage, the sensor ground is open, or a broken signal line floats up through a pull-up inside the module.
s: Warning lamp on
Engine runs on base boost only with reduced power
Live data shows sensor D at maximum even at idle
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance at the connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor D internally failed with output stuck high

P2CDA.d: P2CDA concerns cryogenic fuel storage, in practice liquefied natural gas (LNG) and possibly liquid hydrogen, kept in a double-walled tank whose gap is evacuated. Once that vacuum softens, heat leaks in, the liquid boils faster and pressure climbs until the relief valve vents gas.
s: Tank pressure rises quickly while the vehicle stands, relief valve vents gas
Frost or condensation on the outer tank shell
Fuel loss and shorter standing time after refuelling
c: Vacuum between inner and outer tank wall lost through a leaking weld, fitting or seal
Gradual vacuum decay from outgassing over years of service, tank due for pump-down
Dent or impact damage to the outer shell breaching the insulation space
Pressure rise from another cause (economizer, pressure regulator, sensor) misread as insulation loss

P2CDB.d: P2CDB is part of the monitoring of cold start emission strategies: some engines shut off cylinders or hold intake valves closed right after a cold start to heat the catalyst faster, and CARB requires the commanded elements of such a strategy to be checked while it is active. CARB also asks for faults found during the cold start strategy to carry codes distinct from the ordinary ones, which is why this code exists bes
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Rough running in the first minutes after starting a cold engine
Misfire code for cylinder 1 stored alongside
c: Latch pin of the switchable rocker or lifter on cylinder 1 sticking, often from contaminated oil
Wrong oil grade or low oil level slowing the switching while the oil is still cold
Cylinder 1 control solenoid responding sluggishly at low temperature
Engine control software misjudging the cold start test, cured by an update

P2CDC.d: With P2CDC the control unit reports that cylinder 2 did not take the valve state that the cold start routine asked for. Timing matters here: in a Ford patent on electrically latched rockers, intake deactivation is wanted at engine start, yet the cam of cylinder 2 sits on its lobe, so its latch pin cannot move at first.
s: Uneven idle while the engine warms up
Warning lamp, sometimes with a cylinder 2 misfire code
Engine control may suspend the cold start strategy
c: Latch pin on cylinder 2 seized by dirt or varnish in the oil
Hydraulic lash adjuster pumped up so the rocker stays loaded on base circle
Weak cylinder 2 solenoid or high resistance in its connector
Worn cam lobe or collapsed lifter on cylinder 2

P2CDD.d: P2CDD flags cylinder 3 when its deactivation or intake valve control misbehaves during the cold start phase. No maker documents this code publicly, so the closest evidence comes from neighbouring checks.
s: Malfunction lamp, typically after repeated cold starts
Vibration or rough idle shortly after a cold start
Engine takes longer to settle into normal running
c: Cylinder 3 valves keep opening because the switching element does not unlock
Insufficient oil pressure or flow to the switching gallery right after a cold start
Cylinder 3 control solenoid sticking or leaking internally
Manifold pressure signal biased, so a sealed cylinder looks like it still breathes

P2CDE.d: On a four-cylinder engine cylinder 4 is the last one in the count; P2CDE reports that cylinder 4 did not follow the cold start valve command. Engines may do two different things during a cold start.
s: Harsher cranking or start-up shake
Rough first minute after a cold start
Check engine lamp
c: Switchable rocker or lifter on cylinder 4 not changing state
Cylinder 4 solenoid drawing too little current due to corroded terminals
Aged or overdue engine oil impairing the hydraulic switching when cold
Implausible coolant or oil temperature signal triggering the cold start strategy wrongly

P2CDF.d: P2CDF only occurs on engines with at least five cylinders, mostly V6 and V8 units, and says cylinder 5 did not respond correctly to the cold start deactivation or intake valve command. The Delphi patent behind this idea chooses cylinders that sit farthest from the converter along the exhaust, so less heat is lost in the manifold; in its V8 tests the exhaust ran at least 75 °C hotter at equal load.
s: Lamp on after cold starts, sometimes with a cylinder 5 misfire code
Ticking or tapping valve noise when cold
Rough idle until the engine is warm
c: Deactivation lifter or rocker on cylinder 5 failing to lock or unlock
Restricted oil gallery or screen feeding the switching elements of that bank
Faulty cylinder 5 control valve in the valve lifter oil manifold
Calibration issue in the engine control module

P2CE0.d: P2CE0 closes this series of cold start codes; numbering ends at cylinder 6 although many deactivation engines have eight cylinders. It indicates that cylinder 6 did not reach the valve state demanded during the cold start routine.
s: Rough idle or misfire while warming up
Check engine lamp, often with a cylinder 6 misfire code
Cylinder deactivation may stay disabled afterwards
c: Engine control software that misjudges or mis-times the cold start switching, fixed by reprogramming
Deactivating lifter or rocker on cylinder 6 not switching
Low or delayed oil pressure after a cold start
Cylinder 6 control solenoid or its wiring degraded

P2CE1.d: P2CE1 reports an interrupted circuit at intake air heater C, part of the grid-type pre-heat system a diesel uses to warm the incoming air for cold starts. Volvo and Mack use exactly this code on heavy trucks: their 2019 solution K53338075 for 11, 13 and 16 litre engines, including Mack MP7, MP8 and MP10, from US10+OBD13 onwards lists P2CE1-13, the suffix marking an open circuit, among the pre-heat relay codes.
s: Hard starting and long cranking in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
Engine warning lamp
c: Damaged supply power cable between relay and heater, not always visible on an ohmmeter
Pre-heat relay contacts or output burnt open
Poor terminal tension at the heating element or relay plug
Heating element C itself burnt through

P2CE2.d: P2CE2 is the plausibility test for intake air heater C: the circuit is neither open nor shorted, but current draw, voltage drop or heating effect do not fit the command. Under the heavy-duty OBD rules a glow plug or intake air heater must react properly to commands and its circuit must show plausible current and voltage drop.
s: Longer cranking on cold mornings
White smoke and rough running until warm
Warning lamp without an open or short code for heater C
c: Extra resistance from corroded terminals or a worn supply cable lowering heater current
Pre-heat relay switching with excessive voltage drop
Heating element C aged, drawing current outside the expected window
Weak batteries or poor main ground distorting the current and voltage reading

P2CE3.d: P2CE3 means the signal in the circuit of intake air heater C reads too low, as with the control or feedback line shorted to ground or a relay output pulled down. Volvo uses it with the suffix -11, which in the failure type scheme denotes a ground short.
s: Pre-heat not working, hard cold starts
White smoke after starting in cold weather
Fault lamp on the dash
c: Control or feedback wire of heater C chafed through to ground
Pre-heat relay with an internal fault pulling its output low
Outdated engine management software, addressed by a Volvo update
Moisture or corrosion in the relay connector creating a path to ground

P2CE4.d: P2CE4 is stored when heater C's circuit shows an excessive signal, typically a short to battery voltage on the control line or a relay that remains switched on. Volvo and Mack document it as P2CE4-12, the suffix standing for a short to battery.
s: Batteries drained after the truck has been parked
Hot or discoloured cable near the heater
Warning lamp and possibly hard starting if the heater no longer switches
c: Pre-heat relay contacts welded or stuck closed
Control line of heater C shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Faulty supply power cable or loose bracket mounting affecting the circuit
Engine control module output stage for the relay faulty

P2CE5.d: Two manufacturers use P2CE5, with different meanings. In GM's 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B, sensor C is the downstream relative pressure sensor that reads gauge pressure behind the particulate filter.
s: Warning lamp on, usually after two trips on GM diesels
Particulate filter regeneration may run less accurately or more often
Usually no noticeable change in driving
c: Sensor C zero point drifted (offset at standstill too large)
Condensate or soot in the sensing hose holding pressure
Damaged connector or wiring of a digital sensor C

P2CE6.d: P2CE6 marks a sensor C reading that is electrically valid but physically wrong. GM's 2025 diesel tables use it for a frozen downstream relative pressure signal: during transients, with engine speed changing faster than 150 rpm/s and fuel and airflow also changing quickly, the signal must move; too little variation (25OBDG04B: 0.14 % or less in 40 of 50 samples) sets a two-trip Type B code.
s: Warning lamp on
Particulate filter regenerations triggered too early or too late
Filter monitoring (missing substrate test) cannot complete
c: Sensing hose to sensor C kinked, blocked or disconnected
Condensate or frozen water in the sensing line
Exhaust leak near the measuring point

P2CE7.d: P2CE7 means the raw signal of filter pressure sensor C has dropped below its electrical floor, the typical picture of a signal wire shorted to ground or a lost 5 V supply. GM's 2025 diesel tables, where C is the relative pressure sensor behind the particulate filter, set it when the raw value is under 0.02 % in 158 of 200 samples taken every 12.5 ms with the ignition in range and the engine not cranking; it is Type B
s: Warning lamp on
Live data shows sensor C at minimum regardless of engine load
Regeneration planning relies on a soot model only
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground, often from heat damage near the exhaust
5 V supply to the sensor interrupted
Sensor C internally failed with output stuck low

P2CE8.d: P2CE8 is the high-side electrical fault of filter pressure sensor C: its output sits above the range a working sensor can produce. GM's 2025 diesel tables aim this test at a broken line or a battery-voltage short and set the code when the raw signal of the downstream relative pressure sensor exceeds 99.80 % in 158 of 200 samples (12.5 ms task), Type B with two trips.
s: Warning lamp on
Live data shows sensor C at maximum even at idle
Regeneration requests may become more frequent
c: Sensor ground or signal wire open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor C internally failed with output stuck high

P2CE9.d: P2CE9 catches a sensor C signal that jumps rather than drifts. GM's 2025 diesel tables call this a quick change check: when two consecutive raw samples of the downstream relative pressure sensor differ by more than 20 %, the sample counts as failed, and 99 failures in 200 samples set a Type B code.
s: Warning lamp on, sometimes after rough roads or rain
Pressure value jumps in live data
Fault may disappear and return
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C connector
Harness rubbing through on a bracket or exhaust part
Intermittent internal fault of the sensor

P2CEA.d: Sensor D is the fourth slot for particulate filter pressure and only appears in Ford's 2024–25 petrol OBD summary, which watches a filter on each bank (missing substrate codes P226D and P226E); Ford does not say publicly which letter belongs to which filter or tap. For a digital SENT sensor D, P2CEA covers any circuit failure, monitored without pause with 5 s to register, while lost communication with the same sensor
s: Warning lamp on
Particulate filter monitoring for one bank incomplete
Usually no change in driveability
c: Damaged or corroded connector at sensor D
Harness to sensor D damaged by exhaust heat

P2CEB.d: P2CEB says sensor D reports a pressure that is electrically fine but does not match what the exhaust flow should produce. Ford is the only maker found using it, in its 2024–25 petrol summary for engines with a gasoline particulate filter per bank.
s: Warning lamp on
Missing substrate test for that bank cannot be completed
Usually no noticeable change while driving
c: Sensing hose to sensor D cracked, kinked or disconnected
Condensate in the sensing line after short trips
Sensor D drifted or responding slowly

P2CEC.d: P2CEC is set when an analog filter pressure sensor D delivers less voltage than it can in normal service. In Ford's 2024–25 petrol summary, the only public source using sensor D, the limit is 0.3 V for 5 s, checked continuously alongside the A, B and C sensors of the gasoline particulate filters.
s: Warning lamp on
Live data shows sensor D at minimum
Further 5 V sensor codes if the shared supply is affected
c: Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor D open or pulled down
Sensor D failed with output stuck low

P2CED.d: With P2CED the analog output of filter pressure sensor D lies above its usable top end. Ford's gasoline OBD document for 2024–25, with filters on both banks and up to four pressure sensors, sets the code above 4.73 V lasting 5 s.
s: Warning lamp on
Live data shows sensor D at maximum with the engine at idle
Filter monitoring for that bank incomplete
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor D failed with output stuck high

P2CEE.d: P2CEE stands for brief dropouts or jumps in the sensor D signal that do not last long enough for the low or high codes. Ford's 2024–25 petrol summary includes it in the continuous analog check of its gasoline particulate filter sensors, about 5 s to register, with no separate threshold given.
s: Warning lamp on, sometimes only now and then
Pressure value of sensor D jumps in live data
Possibly stored together with other, unrelated codes after a software issue
c: PCM software setting the code falsely (Ford bulletin 20-2257, F-150 2.7L)
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor D connector
Harness to sensor D chafed or intermittently shorted
Intermittent internal fault of sensor D

P2CEF.d: P2CEF concerns a second thermostat that regulates its own part of the cooling system; stuck open means coolant passes through it before the intended temperature, so that circuit warms too slowly or stays too cool. Lotus documents the code in bulletin 131-26007 for the four-cylinder Emira, where thermostat A is the medium-temperature thermostat: the MIL may light and the driver may see a warning about low coolant temp
s: Engine warning lamp
Low coolant temperature warning or slow warm-up
Weaker cabin heating in cold weather
c: Debris in the coolant holding the thermostat valve off its seat
Worn or leaking wax element, piston no longer returns
Earlier thermostat version superseded by the maker (Mercedes M139)

P2CF0.d: P2CF0 is the closed-side counterpart of P2CEF: auxiliary thermostat A fails to open, so the circuit it governs gets too little flow and its temperature climbs past the regulating point while other parts of the engine may look normal. No manufacturer documents P2CF0 publicly.
s: Engine warning lamp
High temperature in one cooling circuit or an overheating warning
Possible power reduction to protect the engine
c: Wax element lost its charge, thermostat no longer opens
Piston jammed by deposits or debris
Air pocket around the element after a coolant service, so it never sees hot coolant

P2CF1.d: P2CF1 covers a further auxiliary thermostat, labelled B, that stays open, so its loop loses its warm-up phase and runs below the intended temperature. Which loop B controls is the maker's choice: engines with split cooling may regulate head, block, oil or heater flow with separate thermostats, each needing its own temperature sensor for diagnosis.
s: Engine warning lamp
Slow warm-up and higher fuel use in cold weather
Weaker cabin heating
c: Valve held open by debris or a weak return spring
Worn wax element that no longer retracts fully
Temperature sensor of that loop reading too low and faking the fault

P2CF2.d: P2CF2 is logged when auxiliary thermostat B does not open: the temperature in its loop keeps rising beyond the opening point while the controller expects it to level off. The loop assigned to B differs by maker, so the actual consequence can be an overheating cylinder head, hot engine oil or, if B guards a smaller branch, merely a local hot spot that the main gauge does not show.
s: Engine warning lamp
Overheating warning or high oil temperature
Reduced power to protect the engine
c: Leaking wax charge, thermostat stays shut
Piston seized by corrosion or deposits
Temperature sensor of that loop reading too high

P2CF3.d: P2CF3 is set when battery coolant pump A turns more slowly than the controller commands, although it is powered and not fully blocked. Typical reasons are a sluggish bearing, deposits on the impeller, low supply voltage or a pump motor that has lost strength; a faulty speed signal can produce the same picture.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Battery temperature higher than usual
Reduced drive or charging power
c: Battery controller software misreading pump speed (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Worn bearing or deposits slowing the pump
Voltage drop on the pump feed or ground under load
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2CF4.d: P2CF4 is about the power feed of the second battery coolant pump, B: the pump or its control unit sees a supply voltage outside the permitted window, or none at all. Unlike the control-circuit codes P0E1A to P0E1C, which watch the command line, this code looks at the line that actually powers the motor, typically a fused 12 V feed plus ground.
s: MIL or hybrid warning on
Pump B silent when commanded
Charging or drive power limited when the battery warms up
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Corroded connector or poor ground on the pump B supply
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC output dragging the supply down
Internal fault in the pump electronics misreading the supply

P2CF5.d: P2CF5 means battery coolant pump B does not turn at all although it is commanded and powered: the rotor is blocked, or the pump electronics has given up after failed start attempts. A seized bearing, debris or deposits after coolant work, a failed motor winding or frozen coolant in a weak mixture are the usual suspects.
s: Warning lamp for hybrid system or engine
Charging slower or interrupted
Power reduced as battery temperature rises
c: Pump B rotor or bearing seized
Debris or deposits jamming the impeller after coolant work
Pump motor or its electronics failed
Coolant frozen due to insufficient antifreeze

P2CF6.d: P2CF6 reports that battery coolant pump B spins above its commanded speed. Once a centrifugal pump loses its load it accelerates, so the most common explanation is air or a low level in the loop, which the title names directly.
s: Gurgling or whining from the pump area
Coolant level in the battery reservoir drops
MIL or hybrid warning, sometimes without other effect
c: Air left in the battery loop after service or poor bleeding
Leak at a battery coolant tube or joint lowering the level
Impeller slipping on the shaft or broken
False speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2CF7.d: P2CF7 is the underspeed fault of battery coolant pump B: the pump turns, but clearly below the commanded speed for longer than the controller tolerates. Compared with the stall code P2CF5 the rotor is still moving, so friction, a partly obstructed impeller, coolant that is too viscous in the cold or a sagging supply are likelier than a dead motor.
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Battery runs warmer than normal
c: Worn bearing or deposits slowing pump B
Supply voltage of pump B dropping under load
Wrong or aged coolant too viscous at low temperature
Battery controller software misjudging pump speed

P2CF8.d: P2CF8 is raised by the driver of coolant bypass valve D when it measures excessive current or overheats and protects itself. No manufacturer documents P2CF8 publicly, and the meaning of D varies: Ford's 2020–2025 gasoline summaries define valve D as the cabin heating valve and report only the smart driver's circuit fault P26BD, plus P26BF from 2024, while GM's 2019 and 2025 tables use the D stuck codes P26C0/P26C2 fo
s: Engine warning lamp
Cabin heat weak or not adjustable (heater valve)
Engine warms up abnormally if the valve sits in the engine loop
c: Valve stiff or seized, so the motor or solenoid draws excess current
Shorted winding in the valve actuator
Valve wires partly shorted to ground or to each other
Overheated or faulty output stage in the control module

P2CF9.d: P2CF9 applies to belt starter-generator systems whose belt tensioner is moved by an actuator rather than by a spring alone. Patents describe the idea: Ford raises belt tension for engine starts and boost and lowers it while charging (US 9,297,445, with an actuator that falls back to high tension when unpowered); a Hyundai/Kia patent uses a solenoid with three tension stages (US 10,648,544); a later Ford patent switch
s: Belt squeal or slip during automatic restarts
Stop-start or electric assist disabled
MIL or system warning on
c: Broken wire or loose connector in the tensioner drive circuit
Open coil or motor winding in the tensioner actuator
Output stage in the controlling module failed

P2CFA.d: P2CFA is logged when the control line of an electrically adjusted BISG belt tensioner reads too low, typically a ground short or a driver that holds the line down permanently. The tensioner's reaction varies with the design: Ford's patent US 9,297,445 describes an actuator that defaults to high belt tension when power is lost, which protects starts but costs efficiency, while a solenoid unit like the one in Hyundai/K
s: Stop-start no longer active
Belt noise at start or under load
Warning lamp on
c: Tensioner control wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the tensioner actuator
Water or corrosion bridging pins at the actuator plug

P2CFB.d: P2CFB mirrors P2CFA on the high side: the tensioner control circuit of a belt integrated starter generator shows a voltage above the expected range, usually from a wire touching a battery-voltage feed or a driver stage that cannot switch off. The actuator may then be held in one position permanently.
s: Belt slip or squeal at engine start
Faster belt wear or bearing noise
MIL on, stop-start or assist unavailable
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the module unable to switch off
Actuator electronics reporting an implausibly high level

P2CFC.d: P2CFC is the general fault of the output that powers the compressor clutch coil directly, unlike P0645, which covers a clutch relay. Ford is the documented user and runs it in a body module, not the PCM.
s: A/C blows only warm air
Compressor clutch does not engage
Code stored in the HVAC or body control module, usually without engine lamp
c: Spread or pushed-out terminals at the body control module connector
Open or burnt clutch field coil
Damaged wire or connector between module and compressor
Faulty clutch output in the controlling module

P2CFD.d: P2CFD means the voltage on the clutch coil output reads lower than the module expects for the commanded state, most often because the line or the coil is grounded. With a high-side driver that short pulls the feed down, so the clutch cannot engage and the driver may protect itself; on a low-side design a grounded line would hold the clutch in instead.
s: No cooling, compressor clutch stays disengaged
Possibly blown fuse in the clutch feed
c: Clutch feed wire chafed through and touching ground
Damaged terminals at the body control module (Ford SSM 50811/51380)
Clutch coil shorted internally to its housing

P2CFE.d: P2CFE reports a clutch coil output that sits higher than it should, typically because the line touches a battery feed. Then the clutch may stay energized after the module switches off, so the compressor keeps running and can ice the evaporator; a low-side driver instead shuts down and the clutch never engages.
s: Compressor runs even with A/C switched off
Iced evaporator, weak airflow after a while
Alternatively no cooling at all if the driver shuts down
c: Clutch control wire shorted to a battery-powered circuit
Output stage in the module stuck switched on
Moisture bridging pins in the compressor or module connector

P2CFF.d: P2CFF does not come from a voltage comparison but from the protective logic of the clutch output itself. Modern smart switches limit their current and switch off once the junction gets too hot; the TI TPS1HB16-Q1, a typical automotive high-side switch, shuts down from 150 °C and retries within milliseconds, and the module logs this as overcurrent or overtemperature.
s: Cooling cuts in and out
Compressor clutch disengages under load or after warm-up
c: Clutch field coil with shorted turns drawing too much current
Feed wire partly shorted to ground
Output stage overheating from poor module cooling or an internal fault
